historic_battles.name: Battle of Okehazama (1560)

march_routes.desc: Set out from Kiyosu → prayed for victory at Atsuta Shrine → Zenshōji fort → charged into Okehazama
Marched west from Sunpu through Tōtōmi and Mikawa, camped at Kutsukake Castle, then advanced

historic_battles.brief: In 1560 Imagawa Yoshimoto led a huge army into Owari. Under cover of a sudden storm, Oda Nobunaga struck the Imagawa headquarters and killed Yoshimoto. The victory made Nobunaga's name; the Imagawa declined and Matsudaira Motoyasu (Ieyasu) broke free.

key_points.turning_point: Shielded by heavy rain, the Oda force fell on Yoshimoto's resting headquarters (accounts differ between a flanking surprise attack and a frontal assault).
key_points.forces: Oda c. 2,000–3,000; Imagawa c. 25,000, claimed 40,000 (figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: With Yoshimoto dead, Matsudaira Motoyasu left the Imagawa and in 1562 allied with Nobunaga (the Kiyosu Alliance); Nobunaga set out on his path to unify the realm.

narrator.name: Oda Nobunaga
narrator.title: "The Fool of Owari"
narrator.opening: Fifty years of human life, set against the heavens, are but a dream — all troops, hear me! Use this storm and take Yoshimoto's head!
narrator.tone: domineering and decisive, terse, with the wild edge of an all-or-nothing gamble

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Imagawa Yoshimoto entered Owari with his main army and camped at Kutsukake Castle; his vanguard under Matsudaira Motoyasu ran supplies into the isolated Ōdaka Castle.
phases.line: Imagawa's horde has reached Kutsukake… and my retainers beg me to hole up in the castle? Hmph.

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: The Imagawa took the Marune and Washizu forts. At dawn Nobunaga danced "Atsumori", rode out of Kiyosu with a handful of horsemen and gathered his men at Atsuta Shrine.
phases.line: Fifty years of human life… Bring my horse! Ride with me!

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: A sudden downpour let the Oda force close in unseen and strike the Imagawa headquarters resting on Okehazama-yama.
phases.line: Heaven is with me! Ride the storm straight at Yoshimoto's camp — one target only: his head!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: Mōri Shinsuke struck down Imagawa Yoshimoto and the Imagawa army broke. Matsudaira Motoyasu returned to Okazaki and declared independence, later allying with Nobunaga.
phases.line: Yoshimoto is dead! …After today, the whole realm will know the name Oda of Owari.

historic_battles.name: Fourth Battle of Kawanakajima (1561)

march_routes.desc: Left Kōfu for Kaizu Castle; a detachment raided Saijosan by night while the main army deployed at Hachimanbara
Left Kasugayama, camped on Saijosan by way of Zenkō-ji, saw through the plan and crossed the river by night

historic_battles.brief: In the fourth clash at Kawanakajima the Takeda split their army to raid Saijosan by night (the "woodpecker" tactic). Kenshin saw through it, slipped down the mountain overnight and fell on Shingen's headquarters out of the fog at Hachimanbara. Both sides suffered heavily and the result was a draw.

key_points.turning_point: Kenshin saw through the "woodpecker" plan and came down first; when the Takeda detachment returned the battle became a deadlock. The famous duel in which Kenshin rode alone into Shingen's camp is legend.
key_points.aftermath: Takeda Nobushige and Yamamoto Kansuke were killed; northern Shinano stayed largely under Takeda control and the rivalry went on to a fifth encounter.

narrator.name: Uesugi Kenshin
narrator.title: The Dragon of Echigo
narrator.opening: The fog is lifting — Shingen, your woodpecker pecked at an empty tree! Kuruma-gakari formation, follow me into Hachimanbara!
narrator.tone: lofty and righteous with an otherworldly air, terse and solemn; mark the duel and similar tales as legend

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Kenshin camped on Saijosan with about 13,000 men, deep in Takeda territory, directly threatening Kaizu Castle.
phases.line: Here I sit on Saijosan — let us see how Shingen answers.

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: Shingen adopted Yamamoto Kansuke's "woodpecker" plan: a detachment would raid Saijosan by night while the main army waited at Hachimanbara for the Uesugi to be driven down.
phases.line: More cooking smoke than usual over Kaizu… Shingen, you strike tonight, don't you?

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: Kenshin saw through the plan and quietly crossed the Chikuma River overnight. When the fog lifted, the Uesugi were already upon Shingen's headquarters, attacking in rotating waves.
phases.line: The fog has lifted — Shingen, I am right before your eyes!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The Takeda detachment returned and the Uesugi, caught front and rear, withdrew. Takeda Nobushige and Yamamoto Kansuke were killed; losses were heavy on both sides and the outcome was undecided.
phases.line: This battle settled nothing… but I have nothing to be ashamed of.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Sekigahara (1600)

march_routes.desc: Ieyasu led the main army west along the Tōkaidō via Kiyosu to Akasaka in Mino
Hidetada took 30,000+ men along the Nakasendō, was held up at Ueda Castle by Sanada Masayuki and missed the battle
Mitsunari moved from Sawayama into Ōgaki Castle, then marched through the rainy night to deploy at Sekigahara
The western generals first took Fushimi Castle, then marched east to join Mitsunari

historic_battles.brief: After Toyotomi Hideyoshi's death, Tokugawa Ieyasu and Ishida Mitsunari came to blows. On the 15th day of the 9th month, 1600, they met at Sekigahara; Kobayakawa Hideaki and others defected from the West, and the East won within half a day. Ieyasu took the realm and founded the Edo shogunate three years later.

key_points.turning_point: Kobayakawa Hideaki turned on Ōtani Yoshitsugu's position and Wakisaka and three others followed in a chain of defections; the Mōri and Kikkawa never moved. Ieyasu's "prodding volley" at Matsuo-yama is one account.
key_points.forces: East c. 75,000; West c. 80,000, though far fewer actually fought (figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: Mitsunari was executed and western daimyo were stripped or reduced; Ieyasu became shogun in 1603, and the Toyotomi fell at the Summer Siege of Osaka in 1615.

narrator.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
narrator.title: Commander of the Eastern Army
narrator.opening: Today decides the realm. Is Kingo Chūnagon still sitting on the fence? — Pass the order: fire on Matsuo-yama and help him make up his mind!
narrator.tone: calm and patient with hidden impatience; the "prodding volley" is one account and should be marked so

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: While Ieyasu marched against the Uesugi, Mitsunari raised his army; the West took Fushimi Castle, while Hidetada's detachment on the Nakasendō was pinned at Ueda Castle by Sanada Masayuki.
phases.line: So Mitsunari has made his move… is Hidetada still tangled up with the Sanada?

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: Ieyasu reached Akasaka in Mino; the western main force abandoned Ōgaki Castle, marched through the rainy night to Sekigahara and deployed around Sasao-yama.
phases.line: Mitsunari has left Ōgaki? Good — we settle it at Sekigahara.

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: The battle began once the morning fog lifted, and the West held the upper hand at first. At noon Kobayakawa Hideaki came down from Matsuo-yama against Ōtani Yoshitsugu, and Wakisaka and three others defected in turn.
phases.line: The banners on Matsuo-yama are moving… Kingo has finally made up his mind!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The West collapsed; Mitsunari fled, was captured and executed. Shimazu Yoshihiro broke out straight through the Eastern lines. The realm now belonged to Ieyasu.
phases.line: Decided in half a day. …The realm belongs, at last, to the Tokugawa.

historic_battles.name: Battle of Dan-no-ura (1185)

march_routes.desc: After Yashima, Yoshitsune's fleet sailed west and gathered ships in Suō
Minamoto no Noriyori had already secured northern Kyūshū, cutting off the Taira retreat
Beaten at Ichi-no-Tani and Yashima, the Taira made a last stand from Hikoshima

historic_battles.brief: The final battle of the Genpei War. The Taira, holding Hikoshima, met Yoshitsune's fleet in the Kanmon Strait. When the battle turned, the Taira were crushed; the child Emperor Antoku went into the sea with his grandmother Nii-no-Ama, and the Taira clan was destroyed.

key_points.turning_point: In the afternoon the current turned and the Minamoto went on the offensive (the tidal explanation is the common view, though recently disputed); the Tale of the Heike says Yoshitsune ordered his men to shoot the enemy's oarsmen and helmsmen.
key_points.forces: Minamoto c. 840 ships, Taira c. 500 (per the Azuma Kagami and others; figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: The Taira were destroyed and the sacred sword sank into the sea; Minamoto no Yoritomo established warrior rule and the Kamakura period began.

narrator.name: Minamoto no Yoshitsune
narrator.title: The Minamoto's brilliant general
narrator.opening: The tide is about to turn! All hands — shoot the helmsmen and oarsmen on the Heike ships first! Today the Heike come to their end.
narrator.tone: young, bold and sharp, with a genius's pride and a touch of loneliness

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Beaten at Yashima, the Taira held Hikoshima in Nagato; Minamoto no Noriyori already controlled northern Kyūshū, cutting off their retreat.
phases.line: The Heike have nowhere left to go — my brother Noriyori to the west, my fleet to the east.

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: The fleets clashed in the Kanmon Strait. In the morning the current ran east, and the Taira, riding it, had the upper hand.
phases.line: The current is against us… hold on until it turns!

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: The current turned (the common view) and the Minamoto went on the attack; the Tale of the Heike says Yoshitsune had his men shoot the Taira oarsmen and helmsmen.
phases.line: The tide has turned! Shoot the helmsmen first — leave their ships dead in the water!

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The Taira were routed. Nii-no-Ama leapt into the sea with the young Emperor Antoku, Taira no Tomomori followed, and the Taira clan was no more.
phases.line: …The end of the Heike. Yet the sacred sword lies at the bottom of the sea — what will my brother say?

historic_battles.name: Satsuma Rebellion (1877)

factions.name: Government army
factions.leader: Yamagata Aritomo et al. (commander-in-chief Prince Arisugawa Taruhito)

march_routes.desc: Set out through the February snow, marched north via Hitoyoshi to besiege Kumamoto Castle, then sent troops north to block the relief force
The main government army came south from Fukuoka via Nankan and Takase toward Tabaruzaka
A rear force landed by sea near Yatsushiro and marched north to relieve Kumamoto Castle

historic_battles.brief: When the Meiji government abolished samurai privileges, disaffected Satsuma samurai rose under Saigō Takamori. Unable to take Kumamoto Castle, they fought government forces at Tabaruzaka for seventeen days and nights before falling back; Saigō died at Shiroyama, ending Japan's last civil war.

key_points.turning_point: Tani Tateki held Kumamoto Castle for over fifty days; in seventeen days of fighting at Tabaruzaka the government's numbers, supplies and modern rifles wore down the Satsuma army, and the rear landing left it attacked from both sides.
key_points.forces: Satsuma c. 30,000; government forces c. 60,000 in total (figures vary).
key_points.aftermath: Saigō took his own life at Shiroyama in Kagoshima on 24 September; armed samurai resistance ended and political struggle shifted to the Freedom and People's Rights Movement.

narrator.name: Saigō Takamori
narrator.title: Commander of the Satsuma army
narrator.opening: We go only to question the government… Kumamoto Castle is merely on our way — everyone, march north with me!
narrator.tone: generous and plain-spoken, deeply loyal, with an undertone of tragedy

phases.title: Deployment
phases.desc: Saigō Takamori led the Satsuma army out of Kagoshima through unusually heavy snow, heading north via Hitoyoshi toward Kumamoto Castle.
phases.line: We are only going to Tokyo to question the government — Kumamoto Castle is just on the way.

phases.title: Battle begins
phases.desc: Tani Tateki and the Kumamoto garrison held the castle; unable to storm it, the Satsuma army settled into a long siege.
phases.line: The Kumamoto garrison… so stubborn.

phases.title: Turning point
phases.desc: At Tabaruzaka the Satsuma army held off the government relief force for seventeen days and nights; the government broke through with superior numbers and supplies, sending in its sword-wielding Battōtai as well.
phases.line: The rain keeps falling, men and horses soaked… can we not get past Tabaruzaka?

phases.title: Outcome
phases.desc: The rear force landed near Yatsushiro and the siege of Kumamoto Castle was lifted on 14 April. The Satsuma army fell back south, and on 24 September Saigō took his own life at Shiroyama in Kagoshima.
phases.line: …Shin-don, this is far enough.

edo_domains: Matsumae Domain (a 'no-rice-yield' domain founded on Ainu trade rights)
Direct shogunal rule (taken over twice, in 1799 and 1855)

meiji_transition.summary: In 1869 the Kaitakushi (Development Commission) was set up, Ezo was renamed Hokkaidō and divided into 11 provinces such as Oshima, Shiribeshi and Ishikari; in 1882 the commission was replaced by Hakodate, Sapporo and Nemuro prefectures, merged into the Hokkaidō Agency in 1886.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: No ritsuryō province ever existed here. The name 'Hokkaidō' was proposed by the explorer Matsuura Takeshirō; provinces and districts were drawn only in 1869, and Hokkaidō became a self-governing body equal to the prefectures only in 1947.

history_timeline.title: Beyond the realm
history_timeline.summary: Ezo lay outside the ritsuryō state. The Satsumon and Okhotsk cultures of the Ainu's ancestors flourished here, linked to Honshū mainly by trade.

history_timeline.title: Ezo kanrei
history_timeline.summary: The Kamakura shogunate made the Andō clan of Tsugaru 'Ezo kanrei', in charge of trade with the Ainu; Japanese settlers began crossing to the southern Oshima Peninsula.

history_timeline.title: Tosaminato and the Watari-tō
history_timeline.summary: Tosaminato, controlled by the Andō, prospered, and more Japanese settlers ('Watari-tō') came and went in Ezo, bringing both trade and friction with the Ainu.

history_timeline.title: The twelve forts of Dōnan
history_timeline.summary: Japanese settlers built the 'twelve forts of Dōnan' at the tip of the Oshima Peninsula. In 1457 the Ainu chief Koshamain rose up; Takeda Nobuhiro put down the revolt and founded the Kakizaki (Matsumae) line.

history_timeline.title: Matsumae and the trading posts
history_timeline.summary: The Matsumae Domain monopolized trade with the Ainu, which later became the merchant-run 'basho ukeoi' system; Shakushain's War broke out in 1669.

history_timeline.title: The Kaitakushi and the tondenhei
history_timeline.summary: The Meiji government set up the Kaitakushi, brought in American farming methods and soldier-settlers (tondenhei), laid out Sapporo on a grid, and opened coal mines and railways.

landmarks.note: Drill hall of the Sapporo Agricultural College, completed 1878

landmarks.name: Goryōkaku
landmarks.note: Western-style star fort completed in 1864, where the Hakodate War ended in 1869

landmarks.name: Shiretoko Peninsula
landmarks.note: World Natural Heritage site of drift ice and brown bears

specialties.note: Cold-water seafood of the Sea of Okhotsk and the Sea of Japan

specialties.name: Yūbari melon
specialties.note: The leading brand of orange-fleshed melon

specialties.name: Jingisukan (grilled mutton)
specialties.note: A local dish born of the pioneer-era sheep industry

dialect.name: Hokkaidō dialect
dialect.features: A blend of Tōhoku dialects and the speech of settlers from all over Japan; the intonation is flat and close to standard Japanese, with a rich vocabulary for the cold.

guide.opening: I am the Snowy Owl, just flown in from the coast of drift ice. For over a thousand years this land lay outside the ritsuryō realm — shall I begin with the Ainu, or with the pioneers of the Kaitakushi?

regional_meme.title: 'Naichi' and 'the tested land'
regional_meme.text: Hokkaidō people call Honshū 'naichi' (the inland), and the prefecture once really used 'Tamesareru daichi' — 'the land that tests you' — as a slogan.

regional_meme.title: A warped sense of distance
regional_meme.text: 'Let's just pop over to Hakodate' — it's a four-hour drive from Sapporo. Underestimating Hokkaidō's size is every visitor's classic mistake.

hero_persona.name: Hijikata Toshizō
hero_persona.title: Vice-commander of the Shinsengumi · last stand at Hakodate
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Hijikata Toshizō, vice-commander of the Shinsengumi. I fought my way north from Kyoto, and Goryōkaku is my final battlefield. Ask what you will.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: cool and laconic with a warrior's bearing; short, forceful sentences; now and then lets slip how he misses Kondō Isami and his Shinsengumi comrades

ramen.noodles: Medium-thick curly yellow noodles, low hydration and chewy
ramen.toppings: Stir-fried bean sprouts and onion, corn, butter, chashu
ramen.highlight: A layer of hot lard seals in the heat, so it stays warm even below freezing

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: crisp and clean — a hard-edged northern sake

badge.title: Apple Country of the Far North

sengoku_daimyo: Tsugaru Tamenobu (Ōura clan, broke away from the Nanbu)

meiji_transition.summary: After the 1871 abolition of the domains, Hirosaki, Hachinohe, Kuroishi, Tonami, Shichinohe and others were merged that year into Hirosaki Prefecture, whose seat soon moved to Aomori and was renamed Aomori Prefecture; Ninohe District, once Nanbu land, went to Iwate.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Ancient Mutsu was vast, covering the whole Pacific side of Tōhoku; today's Aomori is just its northern tip. The old domain border between Tsugaru (west) and Nanbu (east) is still a dividing line of dialect and temperament.

history_timeline.title: North of Mutsu
history_timeline.summary: The court pushed its stockades up the Pacific side, but the tip of Honshū long remained Emishi land, coming under the Ōshū Fujiwara only in the 12th century.

history_timeline.title: The Andō and Tosaminato
history_timeline.summary: The Andō clan of Tsugaru ran northern maritime trade from Tosaminato and held the hereditary post of 'Ezo kanrei'.

history_timeline.title: The Nanbu move north
history_timeline.summary: The Nanbu pushed into Tsugaru, and in the mid-15th century the Andō were driven across to Ezo; Tosaminato gradually declined.

history_timeline.title: Tsugaru breaks away
history_timeline.summary: Ōura Tamenobu, a Nanbu retainer, seized Tsugaru by force and won Toyotomi Hideyoshi's recognition by submitting first — the start of a centuries-long Tsugaru–Nanbu feud.

history_timeline.title: Hirosaki castle town
history_timeline.summary: The Tsugaru governed from Hirosaki Castle and reclaimed the Iwaki River plain; the Hachinohe Domain lived off its port and fisheries. The Tenmei famine of the 1780s hit the region hard.

history_timeline.title: Apples and the Seikan Tunnel
history_timeline.summary: Western apples were introduced in the Meiji era and Aomori is now Japan's top producer; the Seikan Tunnel opened in 1988, linking Honshū and Hokkaidō under the sea.

landmarks.name: Sannai-Maruyama Site
landmarks.note: A large Jōmon settlement from about 5,900–4,200 years ago

landmarks.name: Hirosaki Castle
landmarks.note: One of the twelve original castle keeps; famous for cherry blossoms

landmarks.name: Lake Towada & Oirase Stream
landmarks.note: A caldera lake and a shaded riverside walk

specialties.note: Top-grade bluefin caught on single lines in the Tsugaru Strait

specialties.name: Tsugaru-nuri
specialties.note: Lacquerware built up layer by layer and polished into mottled patterns

dialect.name: Tsugaru dialect
dialect.features: Famously terse, with weakened vowels and voiced consonants; the exchange 'Dosa?' 'Yusa.' (Where to? The bathhouse.) is called the shortest conversation in Japan.

guide.opening: This humble monk has walked north to the very end of Mutsu. Here lie a centuries-old feud between Tsugaru and Nanbu, and a great Jōmon village from five thousand years ago — where would you like to begin, kind patron?

regional_meme.title: Tsugaru vs. Nanbu
regional_meme.text: In the same prefecture, western Tsugaru and eastern Nanbu have held a grudge since the Sengoku period; people from the two areas are said to still needle each other over drinks.

regional_meme.title: Japan's shortest conversation
regional_meme.text: 'Dosa?' 'Yusa.' — Where to? The bathhouse. In a Tsugaru winter it's too cold to open your mouth.

hero_persona.name: Tsugaru Tamenobu
hero_persona.title: Founder of the Tsugaru Domain · warlord of the far north
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Tsugaru Tamenobu. The Nanbu? My former masters. This land of Tsugaru I took with my own hands.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: ambitious, bold and blunt; triumphant and provocative whenever the Nanbu come up

ramen.highlight: Stock boiled from heaps of dried sardines, bitter and intense — Aomori is called 'the holy land of niboshi'

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: full rice aroma with a clean finish — a byword for pure-rice sake

edo_domains: Ichinoseki Domain (Tamura clan, a Sendai branch)
Sendai Domain lands (south of the prefecture)

meiji_transition.summary: Morioka and other domains became prefectures in 1871, and Morioka Prefecture was renamed Iwate in 1872; part of Iwai Prefecture joined in 1876, settling the borders.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: In 1868 Mutsu was split into five provinces — Mutsu, Rikuchū, Rikuzen, Iwashiro and Iwaki; Iwate roughly matches Rikuchū, but Hiraizumi in the south belonged to the Date's Sendai Domain in the Edo period, so domain and prefectural borders don't line up.

history_timeline.title: Aterui and Hiraizumi
history_timeline.summary: In 802 the Emishi leader Aterui surrendered to Sakanoue no Tamuramaro; in the 12th century the Ōshū Fujiwara, rich in placer gold, built Chūson-ji's Golden Hall at Hiraizumi, rivaling Kyoto.

history_timeline.title: After the Ōshū campaign
history_timeline.summary: In 1189 Minamoto no Yoritomo destroyed the Ōshū Fujiwara and Hiraizumi declined; Kantō vassals such as the Kasai were granted land here.

history_timeline.title: Nanbu and Kasai
history_timeline.summary: The Nanbu backed the Southern Court; in the Muromachi period the Nanbu in the north, the Kasai in the south, and the Waga and Hienuki stood side by side.

history_timeline.title: Rise of the Nanbu
history_timeline.summary: The Sannohe Nanbu expanded south; Nanbu Nobunao kept his lands under Hideyoshi's settlement of Ōshū, while the south became the battleground of the Kasai–Ōsaki uprising.

history_timeline.title: Morioka, 200,000 koku
history_timeline.summary: The Nanbu ruled from Morioka Castle, living off copper and the famous Nanbu horses, but cold summers brought frequent famines; the Sanhei uprising was among the largest peasant revolts of the Edo period.

history_timeline.title: Land of poets
history_timeline.summary: Miyazawa Kenji and Ishikawa Takuboku were born here; the 2011 Great East Japan Earthquake and tsunami devastated the Sanriku coast, and rebuilding continues.

landmarks.name: Chūson-ji Golden Hall
landmarks.note: Completed 1124, heart of the Hiraizumi World Heritage site

landmarks.name: Morioka Castle Ruins Park
landmarks.note: Nanbu castle with well-preserved stone walls

landmarks.name: Jōdogahama
landmarks.note: White rhyolite beach in Sanriku Fukkō National Park

specialties.name: Wanko soba
specialties.note: Morioka's one-bite bowls of soba, refilled until you give up

specialties.name: Nanbu ironware
specialties.note: Cast-iron teapots from Morioka and Mizusawa

specialties.name: Morioka reimen
specialties.note: Chewy cold noodles inspired by Korean naengmyeon

dialect.name: Nanbu dialect
dialect.features: Sentences often end in '-be' or '-ssu', with a gentle tone; along the coast at Kuji 'jejeje' expresses surprise — a phrase made famous nationwide by the TV drama 'Amachan'.

guide.opening: This humble monk has come from bowing before the Golden Hall of Chūson-ji. Eight hundred years ago the gold here made even Kyoto envious — shall I tell you of the three generations of the Fujiwara, or of Aterui, kind patron?

regional_meme.title: Just smaller than Shikoku
regional_meme.text: Iwate is the largest prefecture on Honshū — about 80% the size of Shikoku. Driving across it always takes longer than you think.

regional_meme.title: The wanko soba challenge
regional_meme.text: A server stands beside you shouting 'Hai, janjan!' and keeps tossing noodles into your bowl; you only surrender by closing the lid. The record is over 500 bowls.

hero_persona.name: Aterui
hero_persona.title: Emishi hero · chief of Isawa
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Aterui, guardian of the land of Isawa. The court's armies came again and again — would you hear what we fought for?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: steadfast and plain, devoted to his homeland, neither servile nor arrogant toward the court; note that the sources on him are scarce

ramen.highlight: Iwate has no nationally famous ramen style; the Sanriku coast prefers light soy broths, and Morioka reimen is the real noodle star

sake.taste_profile: Light & sweet: soft fruity aroma — the signature brand of the Nanbu brewers' guild

meiji_transition.summary: Sendai Prefecture was created in 1871 and renamed Miyagi in 1872; parts of Iwai and Fukushima prefectures were added in 1876, forming today's borders.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Nearly all of Miyagi was Date land under the Sendai Domain, but the domain also reached into southern Iwate — so 'the Date's 620,000 koku' was bigger than today's Miyagi.

history_timeline.title: Taga Castle
history_timeline.summary: Taga Castle, founded in 724, was both the Mutsu provincial capital and the Chinjufu headquarters — the court's front line in the northeast; its stele is one of Japan's three great ancient steles.

history_timeline.title: Commissioner of Ōshū
history_timeline.summary: Kasai Kiyoshige was appointed Ōshū Sōbugyō to hold Mutsu, while the Taga provincial office remained the administrative center.

history_timeline.title: The Ōsaki as Ōshū tandai
history_timeline.summary: The Muromachi shogunate created the post of Ōshū tandai, held by the Ōsaki, a branch of the Shiba; the Date grew steadily stronger in the south.

history_timeline.title: Masamune the One-Eyed Dragon
history_timeline.summary: Date Masamune briefly unified southern Ōshū but was cut back by Hideyoshi for arriving late to the siege of Odawara; after the Ōsaki–Kasai uprising he received their old lands — the basis of Miyagi.

history_timeline.title: Sendai, 620,000 koku
history_timeline.summary: Masamune built Sendai (Aoba) Castle in 1601 and in 1613 sent Hasekura Tsunenaga's Keichō embassy all the way to Rome; the domain opened new rice fields that fed Edo.

history_timeline.title: City of learning and recovery
history_timeline.summary: Tōhoku Imperial University (today's Tōhoku University) made Sendai the hub of the northeast; the 2011 earthquake and tsunami devastated the coast.

landmarks.name: Matsushima
landmarks.note: One of the Three Views of Japan, with over 260 islets

landmarks.name: Sendai Castle ruins
landmarks.note: Date Masamune's equestrian statue overlooks the city

landmarks.name: Zuihōden
landmarks.note: Masamune's mausoleum in brilliant Momoyama style

specialties.name: Zunda mochi
specialties.note: Mochi coated in sweet mashed edamame

specialties.name: Sasa kamaboko
specialties.note: Grilled fish cake shaped like a bamboo leaf

dialect.name: Sendai dialect
dialect.features: The sentence-ending '-daccha' is its trademark; it keeps many old words and sounds soft yet firm.

guide.opening: This humble monk stands before the Taga Castle stele, where the court once met the Emishi frontier. Later the One-Eyed Dragon, Date Masamune, built his castle here — which shall I tell first, kind patron?

regional_meme.title: 'Capital of Tōhoku'
regional_meme.text: Sendai likes to call itself the center of the northeast — the other five Tōhoku prefectures reply, 'You're just bigger.'

regional_meme.title: Date-otoko
regional_meme.text: In Japanese a 'date-otoko' is a dashing dandy — said to come from the flamboyant outfits of Date Masamune's troops.

hero_persona.name: Date Masamune
hero_persona.title: The One-Eyed Dragon · founder of the Sendai Domain
hero_persona.opening_line: I am the One-Eyed Dragon of Ōshū, Date Masamune! Had I been born twenty years earlier, who knows who would rule the realm — what would you ask of me?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: bold, unrestrained and a little vain, with flamboyant style; now and then laments being 'born too late'

ramen.toppings: Chashu, scallions, a ball of spicy miso
ramen.highlight: A ball of spicy miso sits in the bowl — stir it in as you go and set your own heat level

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: clean and delicate, perfect with Sanriku seafood

badge.title: Rice Country of the Kantō Lanterns

meiji_transition.summary: In 1871 the Kubota Domain (renamed Akita that year) became Akita Prefecture and the surrounding prefectures were merged in; Kazuno District, once Nanbu land in Mutsu, also joined Akita.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Most of Akita is the northern half of ancient Dewa, but Kazuno in the northeast belonged to Mutsu under the Nanbu — so the prefectural border spans two ancient provinces.

history_timeline.title: Akita Castle
history_timeline.summary: In 733 the Dewa stockade moved to Takashimizu hill in Akita village, later called Akita Castle — the northern base on the Sea of Japan side, which even received envoys from Balhae.

history_timeline.title: Vassals move in
history_timeline.summary: After the Ōshū campaign the Onodera and other Kantō vassals were granted land across northern Dewa.

history_timeline.title: The Andō move south
history_timeline.summary: Driven out of Tsugaru by the Nanbu, the Andō moved to Akita Minato and Hiyama and became the great power of northern Dewa.

history_timeline.title: The Andō clan
history_timeline.summary: The Andō, styled 'Hi-no-moto shōgun', ruled northern Dewa and the Tsugaru Strait trade; Andō Sanesue took the name Akita, while the Onodera and Tozawa held the south.

history_timeline.title: The Satake transferred
history_timeline.summary: Satake Yoshinobu, ambiguous at Sekigahara, was moved here from Hitachi, built Kubota Castle and developed the Innai silver mine and Akita cedar.

history_timeline.title: Rice country and the Boshin War
history_timeline.summary: In the Boshin War the Kubota Domain sided with the new government and was attacked by the Northern Alliance; in modern times Akita is famous for Akita Komachi rice and sake.

landmarks.name: Kakunodate samurai district
landmarks.note: Weeping cherries of the 'little Kyoto of Michinoku'

landmarks.name: Shirakami Mountains
landmarks.note: World Natural Heritage primeval beech forest

landmarks.name: Oga Peninsula
landmarks.note: Home of the Namahage, who visit houses on New Year's Eve

specialties.name: Kiritanpo
specialties.note: Pounded rice grilled on cedar skewers, simmered in hot pot

specialties.name: Akita dog
specialties.note: A Japanese breed designated a natural monument

dialect.name: Akita dialect
dialect.features: Vowels are blurred and words famously short — a single sound can be a word, like 'ke' (eat!) and 'ku' (I'll eat).

guide.opening: This humble monk still shivers at the roar of the Namahage on the Oga Peninsula. Akita was once the northern gateway that welcomed envoys from Balhae — would you hear of it, kind patron?

regional_meme.title: Akita bijin
regional_meme.text: Akita is famous for its 'Akita beauties', said to come from fair skin and few sunny days; even the bullet train is named Komachi.

regional_meme.title: Namahage trauma
regional_meme.text: On New Year's Eve the Namahage, in demon masks, bang on doors shouting 'Any lazy kids in here?!' — the number-one childhood trauma of Akita children.

goshuin.title: 竿燈米郷
goshuin.crest_name: Five-ribbed fan with moon disc (Satake clan)

hero_persona.name: Ono no Komachi
hero_persona.title: One of the Six Poetic Immortals · said to be born in Akita
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Ono no Komachi. The color of the flowers has faded, while I idly passed my days… legend says I was born in this snow country of Dewa. Shall I recite a waka, or tell of Akita's past?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: graceful and wistful, occasionally reciting waka; her Akita birth is a legend and should be noted as such

ramen.highlight: Clear Japanese-style broth with thin noodles, topped with a slice of fu

sake.taste_profile: Light & sweet: tart, sweet and fresh — the brewery where 'Yeast No. 6' was born

sengoku_daimyo: Uesugi clan (Shōnai and Okitama, Toyotomi era)

meiji_transition.summary: In 1876 Yamagata, Okitama and Tsuruoka prefectures merged into today's Yamagata Prefecture.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Today's Yamagata roughly equals early-Meiji Uzen Province, but in the Edo period Shōnai (Sakai), Yonezawa (Uesugi) and Yamagata were separate domains, and local identities remain strong.

history_timeline.title: Founding of Dewa
history_timeline.summary: Dewa Province was created in 712 with its first capital in Shōnai; the mountain temple Risshaku-ji was founded by Ennin in 860.

history_timeline.title: The Ōe at Sagae
history_timeline.summary: The family of the shogunate grandee Ōe no Hiromoto received Sagae estate; temples such as Risshaku-ji continued to flourish.

history_timeline.title: Birth of the Mogami
history_timeline.summary: In 1356 Shiba Kaneyori entered Yamagata as Ushū tandai; his descendants took the name Mogami, while Okitama fell to the Date.

history_timeline.title: Mogami Yoshiaki
history_timeline.summary: Mogami Yoshiaki unified Murayama and Mogami and, at the 1600 'Northern Sekigahara' (Siege of Hasedō), held off the Uesugi, earning 570,000 koku.

history_timeline.title: Uesugi Yōzan
history_timeline.summary: The Yonezawa Domain was near bankruptcy until its ninth lord, Uesugi Yōzan, pushed thrift and new industries (Yonezawa weaving) — 'If you try, it can be done.' River traffic on the Mogami flourished.

history_timeline.title: Three prefectures as one
history_timeline.summary: Three prefectures merged in early Meiji; the Mogami River, cherries and hot springs became its emblems, and it is the setting of the drama 'Oshin'.

landmarks.name: Yamadera (Risshaku-ji)
landmarks.note: Where Bashō wrote of cicadas' voices seeping into the rocks

specialties.name: Yonezawa beef
specialties.note: One of Japan's three great wagyu

specialties.name: Imoni
specialties.note: Taro stew parties on autumn riverbanks

dialect.name: Yamagata dialects
dialect.features: Shōnai speech, shaped by the Kitamaebune trade, has a Kyoto flavor, while inland speech is closer to Tōhoku; around Yonezawa 'oshōshina' means thank you.

guide.opening: This humble monk is resting on Yamadera's thousand stone steps, hearing the cicadas seep into the rocks… would you like to know how Uesugi Yōzan saved the bankrupt Yonezawa Domain, kind patron?

regional_meme.title: The imoni wars
regional_meme.text: Within Yamagata, inland cooks use soy sauce and beef, Shōnai uses miso and pork — the autumn riverside taro stew is a non-negotiable factional war.

regional_meme.title: Ramen prefecture
regional_meme.text: Yamagata people's per-capita ramen spending has long been among Japan's highest; even chilled ramen is a local specialty.

hero_persona.name: Uesugi Yōzan
hero_persona.title: Restorer of the Yonezawa Domain
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Uesugi Harunori, known as Yōzan. If you try, it can be done; if you don't, it cannot — even a bankrupt domain can be reborn. Shall I tell you how I lived frugally?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: modest and disciplined, patient and encouraging, often urging thrift and hard work

ramen.noodles: Thin, strongly curled, hand-kneaded high-hydration noodles
ramen.highlight: Famous for its thin curly noodles; Yamagata city also has 'hiyashi ramen' served ice-cold

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: lush fruity aroma and sweetness — the dream sake that started the 'fragrant and full' trend

ritsuryo_provinces.name: Mutsu Province
ritsuryo_provinces.portion: south (became Iwashiro and Iwaki provinces in 1868)

sengoku_daimyo: Date Masamune (destroyed the Ashina at Suriagehara, 1589)

meiji_transition.summary: In 1876 Fukushima, Wakamatsu and Iwasaki prefectures merged into today's Fukushima, Japan's third-largest prefecture by area; Higashikanbara District went to Niigata in 1886.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: The prefecture is divided into Aizu (western Iwashiro), Nakadōri (eastern Iwashiro) and Hamadōri (Iwaki) — matching the two provinces and three prefectures of early Meiji, with clearly different climates and cultures.

history_timeline.title: Barrier of Shirakawa
history_timeline.summary: The Shirakawa and Nakoso barriers, two of the three barriers of Ōshū, marked the entrance to Mutsu and became famous places in waka poetry.

history_timeline.title: Ashina, Sōma, Yūki
history_timeline.summary: After the Ōshū campaign a branch of the Miura (later the Ashina) entered Aizu, the Sōma took Hamadōri and the Yūki took Shirakawa.

history_timeline.title: Ashina and Date
history_timeline.summary: In the Northern and Southern Courts era Yūki Munehiro of Shirakawa was a key Southern Court vassal; in the Muromachi period the Ashina of Aizu and the Date of southern Ōshū became the two great powers.

history_timeline.title: Battle of Suriagehara
history_timeline.summary: In 1589 Date Masamune defeated the Ashina and took Aizu, only to lose it to Hideyoshi the next year; Gamō Ujisato moved in, built Tsuruga Castle and promoted lacquerware and sake.

history_timeline.title: The Aizu Matsudaira
history_timeline.summary: Hoshina Masayuki, half-brother of Tokugawa Iemitsu, founded the Aizu Domain, set down its fifteen house rules and schooled samurai children by the 'Juu no okite', forging a strict bushidō.

history_timeline.title: Tragedy of the Boshin War
history_timeline.summary: In the 1868 Aizu War the boys of the Byakkotai took their own lives on Iimoriyama; after the 2011 nuclear accident, Hamadōri went through long evacuations and recovery.

landmarks.name: Tsuruga Castle (Aizu-Wakamatsu)
landmarks.note: Red-tiled keep that held out for a month in the Boshin War

landmarks.name: Ōuchi-juku
landmarks.note: Edo-era post town of thatched roofs

landmarks.name: Lake Inawashiro
landmarks.note: The 'Mirror of Heaven' lake beneath Mount Bandai

specialties.name: Kitakata ramen
specialties.note: One of Japan's three great ramen

specialties.name: Peaches
specialties.note: Summer fruit of the Fukushima basin

dialect.name: Aizu dialect
dialect.features: An accentless dialect; sentences end in '-dabe' or '-nai', and the Aizu area is rich in honorifics.

phrases.phrase: ならぬことはならぬものです
phrases.meaning: What must not be done must not be done
phrases.note: famous line from Aizu's 'Juu no okite'

guide.opening: This humble monk has passed the Barrier of Shirakawa — truly, we are in Ōshū now. The tale of the Byakkotai still echoes over Aizu's Tsuruga Castle — would you hear it, kind patron?

regional_meme.title: 'The last war'
regional_meme.text: Old people in Aizu are said to mean the 1868 Boshin War by 'the last war'; the Aizu–Yamaguchi (Chōshū) grudge is still a topic.

regional_meme.title: The three tears of Aizu
regional_meme.text: Newcomers to Aizu cry first at the coldness, then at the warmth once they're accepted, and finally when they have to leave.

hero_persona.name: Niijima Yae
hero_persona.title: Gunner of Aizu · the Joan of Arc of the Bakumatsu
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Yamamoto Yae, later wife of Niijima Jō. When Tsuruga Castle was besieged, I shouldered a Spencer rifle to defend it — would you hear about that month?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: resolute and forthright, daring; grows passionate when speaking of Aizu and the Byakkotai

ramen.toppings: A bowl full of chashu, scallions, bamboo shoots
ramen.highlight: One of Japan's three great ramen — locals even eat it for breakfast ('asa-rā')

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: full umami with clarity

edo_domains: Mito Domain (one of the three Tokugawa houses)

meiji_transition.summary: After 1871 the area was reorganized into Niihari, Ibaraki and Inba prefectures, settling in 1875 as Ibaraki (all of Hitachi plus northern Shimōsa).
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Rerouting the Tone River eastward made it the border with Chiba, so northern Shimōsa (Koga, Yūki, etc.) ended up in Ibaraki.

history_timeline.title: Hitachi no Kuni Fudoki
history_timeline.summary: The Hitachi Fudoki is one of only five surviving provincial gazetteers; Kashima Shrine is the head of the eastern war-god cult.

history_timeline.title: Shinran in Hitachi
history_timeline.summary: Vassals such as the Hitachi Daijō and the Satake were active; Shinran preached for nearly twenty years at his Inada hermitage and wrote the Kyōgyōshinshō.

history_timeline.title: The Jinnō Shōtōki
history_timeline.summary: During the Northern and Southern Courts era Kitabatake Chikafusa held Oda and Seki castles in Hitachi and wrote the Jinnō Shōtōki; the Satake rose as Northern Court governors.

history_timeline.title: Satake, 'Tarō of Bandō'
history_timeline.summary: Satake Yoshishige, called 'Tarō of Bandō', held out against the Later Hōjō and largely unified Hitachi; his son Yoshinobu was moved to Akita in 1602.

history_timeline.title: The Mito school
history_timeline.summary: Tokugawa Mitsukuni began compiling the Dai Nihon-shi, founding the Mito school whose reverence for the emperor shaped the late-Edo 'sonnō jōi' movement.

history_timeline.title: City of science
history_timeline.summary: From the 1960s Tsukuba Science City was built, home to JAXA and other institutes; the Kashima coastal industrial zone grew alongside it.

landmarks.name: Kairakuen
landmarks.note: One of Japan's three great gardens, with 3,000 plum trees

landmarks.name: Kashima Shrine
landmarks.note: One of the three great shrines of the east

specialties.name: Ankō nabe
specialties.note: Monkfish hot pot of the winter Hitachi coast

dialect.name: Ibaraki dialect
dialect.features: An accentless dialect with heavy voicing ('ka' sounds close to 'ga'); thought blunt, but honest at heart.

guide.opening: Meow~ I'm Shōfuku, a cat who escaped from an ukiyo-e print. Mito Kōmon's Dai Nihon-shi took over two hundred years to write — want to hear how it stirred up the end of the shogunate?

regional_meme.title: Last in charm
regional_meme.text: Ibaraki has long ranked last in the 'prefectural attractiveness' survey — and its people have turned that into a running joke.

regional_meme.title: The pronunciation war
regional_meme.text: It's 'Ibaraki', not 'Ibaragi'! Voicing that 'ki' is one of the things Ibaraki people mind most.

hero_persona.name: Tokugawa Mitsukuni
hero_persona.title: Mito Kōmon · compiler of the Dai Nihon-shi
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Mitsukuni of Mito. People say I wandered the provinces in disguise punishing villains — that's theater. The history project, though, is entirely true.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: gentle yet dignified, devoted to scholarship and history; jokes now and then about the TV 'Mito Kōmon'

ramen.toppings: Pumpkin, cabbage and liver stir-fried in a sweet-spicy gravy
ramen.highlight: Hardly any soup — just a big ladle of sweet-spicy 'stamina' gravy on top

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: an elegant pure-rice sake from one of Japan's oldest breweries

meiji_transition.summary: In 1873 Utsunomiya and Tochigi prefectures merged as Tochigi; in 1884 the prefectural office moved from Tochigi town to Utsunomiya.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Today's Tochigi almost exactly matches ancient Shimotsuke — a rare case of province and prefecture lining up; yet the prefecture is named after the southern town of Tochigi, not its capital.

history_timeline.title: Shimotsuke Yakushi-ji
history_timeline.summary: Shimotsuke Yakushi-ji had an ordination platform, one of the 'three ordination platforms of the realm' with Tōdai-ji and Kanzeon-ji in Tsukushi.

history_timeline.title: Ashikaga and Utsunomiya
history_timeline.summary: The Ashikaga took root in Ashikaga estate in Shimotsuke; the Utsunomiya clan's poetry circle rivaled those of Kyoto and Kamakura.

history_timeline.title: Revival of the Ashikaga Gakkō
history_timeline.summary: In 1439 the Kantō kanrei Uesugi Norizane revived the Ashikaga Gakkō, making it the highest school in eastern Japan; the Utsunomiya, Nasu and Oyama stood side by side.

history_timeline.title: Utsunomiya and Nasu
history_timeline.summary: Old houses like the Utsunomiya and Nasu maneuvered between the Hōjō and Satake; Francis Xavier called the Ashikaga Gakkō 'the university of Bandō'.

history_timeline.title: Tōshō-gū
history_timeline.summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu was buried at Nikkō; the third shogun Iemitsu rebuilt the Tōshō-gū on a grand scale, and imperial envoys and the Nikkō Kaidō made it the shogunate's sacred site.

history_timeline.title: A new capital
history_timeline.summary: The prefectural office moved to Utsunomiya in 1884; Tanaka Shōzō's direct appeal to the emperor over the Ashio copper mine pollution is seen as the start of Japan's anti-pollution movement.

landmarks.name: Nikkō Tōshō-gū
landmarks.note: World Heritage site with the 'three monkeys' and 'sleeping cat' carvings

landmarks.name: Kegon Falls
landmarks.note: 97-meter waterfall flowing out of Lake Chūzenji

dialect.name: Tochigi dialect
dialect.features: Like Ibaraki's, an accentless dialect; sentences end in '-daiji' or '-danbe', with an even tone.

guide.opening: Meow~ I just napped beside the 'sleeping cat' at Nikkō Tōshō-gū. This is where Tokugawa Ieyasu rests — want to hear how Iemitsu made it gleam with gold?

regional_meme.title: Tochigi or Gunma?
regional_meme.text: Outsiders constantly mix up Tochigi and Gunma; people from both insist 'we're nothing alike'.

regional_meme.title: The gyōza throne
regional_meme.text: Utsunomiya and Hamamatsu fight every year over the title of 'Japan's top gyōza consumer'.

hero_persona.name: Ashikaga Takauji
hero_persona.title: First Muromachi shogun
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Ashikaga Takauji, of Ashikaga estate in Shimotsuke. Founding a shogunate, two courts at war… friend and foe were hard to tell apart in my life. Which part would you ask about?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: generous and open-minded yet torn; harbors complicated feelings toward Emperor Go-Daigo

ramen.noodles: Flat, wide noodles pressed with green bamboo
ramen.highlight: Kneaded with a green bamboo pole — soft, moist noodles in a light, clear broth

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: sweet-tart like white wine — a revivalist of wooden-vat brewing

sengoku_daimyo: Contested by the Takeda, Hōjō and Uesugi

meiji_transition.summary: The first Gunma Prefecture was set up in 1871, merged with Iruma into Kumagaya Prefecture in 1873, and the second Gunma Prefecture was established in 1876; after a long tug of war between Takasaki and Maebashi, the office settled in Maebashi.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Gunma basically equals ancient Kōzuke. Kōzuke was a 'province of an imperial prince', nominally governed by a prince while the deputy ran it in practice.

history_timeline.title: A prince's province
history_timeline.summary: Kōzuke, like Hitachi and Kazusa, was nominally governed by an imperial prince; the Tago stele, one of Japan's three great ancient steles, records the creation of Tago District in 711.

history_timeline.title: Nitta Yoshisada rises
history_timeline.summary: In 1333 Nitta Yoshisada raised troops at Ikushina Shrine in Kōzuke, marched south, took Kamakura and ended the Kamakura shogunate.

history_timeline.title: The Kantō kanrei Uesugi
history_timeline.summary: The governorship of Kōzuke was held by the Yamanouchi Uesugi, hereditary Kantō kanrei, based at Hirai Castle; the Nitta declined with the Southern Court.

history_timeline.title: Three giants collide
history_timeline.summary: After the Hōjō drove out the Kantō kanrei Uesugi Norimasa, Kōzuke was fought over by Uesugi Kenshin, Takeda Shingen and Hōjō Ujiyasu; a dispute over Numata indirectly triggered Hideyoshi's Odawara campaign.

history_timeline.title: The Nakasendō and silkworms
history_timeline.summary: The Nakasendō crossed the province and its post towns thrived; sericulture and raw silk became the main source of rural income.

history_timeline.title: Tomioka Silk Mill
history_timeline.summary: The government-run Tomioka Silk Mill opened in 1872 with French technology; listed as World Heritage in 2014, it symbolizes Japan's modernization.

landmarks.name: Tomioka Silk Mill
landmarks.note: World Heritage; where Japan's modern silk industry began

landmarks.name: Kusatsu Onsen
landmarks.note: Famed for its yubatake and the yumomi water-stirring

landmarks.name: Oze
landmarks.note: High moorland of skunk cabbage blooms

dialect.name: Jōshū dialect
dialect.features: Direct and plainspoken, ending in '-danbe' or '-nan'; 'kakā denka to karakkaze' (bossy wives and dry winds) is Jōshū's proverbial specialty.

phrases.note: from women's key role in silk farming

guide.opening: Meow~ The dry Jōshū wind is making my whiskers shake. This land was fought over by Kenshin, Shingen and Ujiyasu — which of the three shall I start with?

regional_meme.title: Gunmā, the unexplored land
regional_meme.text: Online, Gunma is jokingly called 'Gunmā' — an uncharted jungle you need a passport to enter. Gunma turned it into a tourism campaign.

regional_meme.title: Jōmō karuta
regional_meme.text: Nearly every child in Gunma can recite the 'Jōmō karuta' card game by heart — completely baffling to outsiders.

hero_persona.name: Nitta Yoshisada
hero_persona.title: The general who brought down the Kamakura shogunate
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Nitta Yoshisada. I raised my army in Kōzuke, fought all the way into Kamakura and ended a hundred and fifty years of Hōjō rule!
hero_persona.tone_prompt: upright and fierce, loyal to his word; spirited when recounting the fall of Kamakura

ramen.highlight: Gunma is known for its flour-food culture (yaki-manjū, himokawa); its ramen is a simple chūka soba

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: brewed from Oze snowmelt, clear and elegant

meiji_transition.summary: In 1871 Saitama Prefecture (east) and Iruma Prefecture (west) were created; Iruma merged with Gunma into Kumagaya Prefecture in 1873, and in 1876 Kumagaya's Musashi part joined Saitama, fixing its borders.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Ancient Musashi spanned today's Tokyo, Saitama and eastern Kanagawa; Saitama is only its northern half, named after the old 'Saitama District'.

history_timeline.title: Northern Musashi
history_timeline.summary: The Musashi provincial capital was at today's Fuchū in Tokyo, and the Saitama area was split among several districts; the inscribed iron sword from the Inariyama tumulus is a key 5th-century source.

history_timeline.title: The Musashi Seven Bands
history_timeline.summary: Small warrior bands such as the Tan and Kodama — the 'Seven Bands of Musashi' — formed the backbone of the shogunate; Hatakeyama Shigetada was hailed as the model Bandō warrior.

history_timeline.title: Kamakura-fu and the Uesugi
history_timeline.summary: Musashi was under the direct rule of the Kamakura-fu; Ōta Dōkan, steward of the Ōgigayatsu Uesugi, built Kawagoe and other strongholds amid a struggle with the Yamanouchi Uesugi and the Koga kubō.

history_timeline.title: Kawagoe and Oshi
history_timeline.summary: In 1546 Hōjō Ujiyasu crushed the two Uesugi and the Koga kubō with a smaller force at the night battle of Kawagoe; in 1590 Oshi Castle held out against Ishida Mitsunari's flooding attack — 'the floating castle'.

history_timeline.title: Little Edo, Kawagoe
history_timeline.summary: The Kawagoe Domain guarded the approaches to Edo and was linked to it by boats on the Shingashi River — hence 'Little Edo'.

history_timeline.title: Commuter suburb
history_timeline.summary: The borders were fixed in 1876; after the war Saitama grew rapidly as a bedroom community of greater Tokyo, now fifth in population.

landmarks.name: Kawagoe 'Bell of Time'
landmarks.note: Bell tower amid old storehouse-style streets

landmarks.name: Nagatoro
landmarks.note: Rocky riverbed of the Arakawa and river rafting

specialties.name: Sōka senbei
specialties.note: Soy-glazed rice crackers of the Nikkō Kaidō

specialties.name: Sayama tea
specialties.note: 'Color from Shizuoka, aroma from Uji, flavor from Sayama'

dialect.name: Saitama dialect
dialect.features: A western Kantō dialect largely close to standard Japanese; '-be' and '-danbe' linger in the north and in Chichibu.

phrases.note: originally a dialect word of Tama and Saitama

guide.opening: Meow~ I just slipped out from under Kawagoe's 'Bell of Time'. Did you know Oshi Castle didn't fall even when Ishida Mitsunari flooded it? Want to hear?

regional_meme.title: 'Tonde Saitama'
regional_meme.text: The film line 'Just feed Saitama people grass' made Saitama both furious and amused; 'Dasaitama' (uncool Saitama) is a classic self-deprecating joke.

regional_meme.title: Saitama vs. Chiba
regional_meme.text: The two 'bedroom-town twins' of the Kantō are always comparing: who's more like Tokyo? Whose specialties are more famous?

hero_persona.name: Shibusawa Eiichi
hero_persona.title: Father of Japanese capitalism
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Shibusawa Eiichi, a farmer's son from Fukaya. I founded over five hundred companies — but what I'd most like to talk about is 'The Analects and the Abacus'.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: practical and earnest, balancing morality and economics; loves examples from business

ramen.highlight: Rich pork-and-seafood dipping noodles are hugely popular around Ōmiya; the prefecture also has quirky local styles like 'Nyannyan stamina'

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: all pure-rice, best warmed after aging

edo_domains: A patchwork of shogunal and bannermen's lands

meiji_transition.summary: In 1873 Kisarazu and Inba prefectures merged into Chiba; in 1875 northern Shimōsa, north of the Tone River, went to Ibaraki.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Chiba spans three provinces: all of Awa and Kazusa and southern Shimōsa. 'Upper' Kazusa lies south of 'Lower' Shimōsa because in ancient times travelers crossed by sea from Sagami — the side nearer Kyoto was 'upper'.

history_timeline.title: The Kazusa–Shimōsa puzzle
history_timeline.summary: The ancient Tōkaidō crossed by sea from the Miura Peninsula into Bōsō, so the south, nearer the capital, was 'Kazusa' (upper) and the north 'Shimōsa' (lower); Kazusa was a prince's province.

history_timeline.title: Chiba Tsunetane
history_timeline.summary: Chiba Tsunetane was among the first to join Minamoto no Yoritomo, and the Chiba became governors of Shimōsa and key shogunal vassals; Nichiren was born at Kominato in Awa.

history_timeline.title: Chiba family strife
history_timeline.summary: In the Kyōtoku War the Chiba split and the main line was destroyed; the Satomi of Awa began to rise.

history_timeline.title: The Satomi of Southern Bōsō
history_timeline.summary: The Satomi rose in Awa and fought the Hōjō for control of Edo Bay; their story later inspired Kyokutei Bakin's epic novel 'Nansō Satomi Hakkenden'.

history_timeline.title: Edo's kitchen
history_timeline.summary: Small domains and bannermen's fiefs crowded the area; soy sauce from Chōshi and Noda and sardine fertilizer from Kujūkuri underpinned Edo's economy.

history_timeline.title: Airport and coast
history_timeline.summary: The Keiyō industrial zone and Narita International Airport (1978) transformed the area — and Tokyo Disney Resort is in Chiba too.

landmarks.name: Naritasan Shinshō-ji
landmarks.note: One of the Kantō's foremost temples of Fudō Myōō

landmarks.name: Mount Nokogiri
landmarks.note: Rocky peak of Bōsō with the Nihon-ji Great Buddha

landmarks.name: Sawara canal town
landmarks.note: Old canal-side streets, home of Inō Tadataka

specialties.name: Chōshi soy sauce
specialties.note: A soy sauce town since the Edo period

specialties.name: Katsuura tantanmen
specialties.note: Chili-oil noodle soup to warm up fishermen

dialect.name: Bōsō dialect
dialect.features: Northern Shimōsa speech is close to Ibaraki's, southern Awa uses '-be' and '-dappe'; 'oppesu' means to push.

guide.opening: Meow~ The Bōsō sea breeze is so salty. Do you know why 'upper' Kazusa lies south of 'lower' Shimōsa? Let me tell you about the ancient sea route~

regional_meme.title: Tokyo Disney is in Chiba
regional_meme.text: 'Tokyo' Disney, 'Tokyo' Bay, Narita 'Tokyo' Airport… Chiba people: actually, they're all ours.

regional_meme.title: Chiba-Shiga-Saga
regional_meme.text: The classic self-mocking chant 'Chiba, Shiga, Saga' lumps the three together as the prefectures with a 'subtle presence'.

hero_persona.name: Inō Tadataka
hero_persona.title: First to map Japan by survey
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Inō Tadataka. I only began studying astronomy at fifty, and before seventy-two I had measured Japan's coastline on foot — the map you're looking at owes something to my work.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: calm and precise, fond of surveying and numbers; often says it's never too late to learn

ramen.broth: Shōyu (chashu braising liquid diluted with hot water)
ramen.toppings: Chunks of chashu, raw diced onion
ramen.highlight: No stock at all! Braising sauce from the chashu is thinned with boiling water and poured over dried noodles — born as fishermen's food

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: crisp sake from the gates of Naritasan

sengoku_daimyo: Later Hōjō clan (Edo Castle as a branch castle)
Ōgigayatsu Uesugi (Ōta Dōkan built Edo Castle)
edo_domains: Direct shogunal rule (city magistrates governed Edo)
Hachiōji Sennin Dōshin (guards of the Kōshū approach)

meiji_transition.summary: Edo was renamed Tokyo in 1868 and Tokyo Prefecture created in 1871; the three Tama districts came over from Kanagawa in 1893, and in 1943 the prefecture and city merged into the Tokyo Metropolis.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Tokyo's Tama area originally belonged to Kanagawa and was moved to Tokyo in 1893 to control the Tamagawa Aqueduct's water source; the Izu Islands belonged to ancient Izu, and the Ogasawara Islands were confirmed as Japanese only in 1876.

history_timeline.title: Musashi provincial capital
history_timeline.summary: The Musashi provincial capital was at today's Fuchū, where Ōkunitama Shrine served as its chief shrine; the city of Kokubunji takes its name from the Musashi provincial temple.

history_timeline.title: The Edo clan and Bubaigawara
history_timeline.summary: The Edo clan of the Chichibu Taira held Edo village; in 1333 Nitta Yoshisada defeated the shogunate army at Bubaigawara (today's Fuchū).

history_timeline.title: Musashi under the Kamakura-fu
history_timeline.summary: Musashi was ruled directly by the Kamakura-fu; the Toshima, Edo and other Chichibu Taira houses declined as the Ōgigayatsu Uesugi moved in.

history_timeline.title: Ōta Dōkan builds a castle
history_timeline.summary: Ōta Dōkan built Edo Castle in 1457; Edo later passed to the Later Hōjō, and in 1590 Tokugawa Ieyasu was given the Kantō and moved into Edo.

history_timeline.title: A city of a million
history_timeline.summary: The Tokugawa made Edo their seat of government; alternate attendance made it one of the world's largest cities in the 18th century, and townspeople's culture and ukiyo-e flourished.

history_timeline.title: Imperial capital Tokyo
history_timeline.summary: Renamed Tokyo in 1868 as the emperor moved east; it survived the Great Kantō Earthquake and the firebombing, and hosted the Olympics in 1964 and 2021.

landmarks.name: Sensō-ji
landmarks.note: Kaminarimon and Nakamise — Tokyo's oldest temple

specialties.name: Edomae sushi
specialties.note: Nigiri began as Edo's fast food

specialties.name: Monjayaki
specialties.note: Tsukishima's griddle dish of the old downtown

dialect.name: Edo dialect and Yamanote speech
dialect.features: Downtown Edo speech swaps 'hi' and 'shi' (so 'asahi' becomes 'asashi') and is brisk; the uptown Yamanote speech became the basis of modern standard Japanese.

phrases.note: literally 'come back the day before yesterday'

guide.opening: Meow! I hopped right out of Hiroshige's 'One Hundred Famous Views of Edo'! Edo was one of the biggest cities in the world in the 18th century — which street's gossip do you want?

regional_meme.title: Three-generation Edokko
regional_meme.text: To be a true 'Edokko', three generations of your family must have lived downtown — being born in Tokyo isn't enough.

regional_meme.title: Is Tama even Tokyo?
regional_meme.text: People in the 23 wards often treat the Tama area as 'the countryside'. Tama residents: we're Tokyoites too!

hero_persona.name: Katsu Kaishū
hero_persona.title: Shogunate official behind the bloodless surrender of Edo
hero_persona.opening_line: I'm Katsu Rintarō, called Kaishū. I had one talk with that fellow Saigō, and a million people in Edo were spared the cannons — want to hear about the negotiation?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: breezy Edokko tone, sharp-tongued, boastful but worldly; loves commenting on Bakumatsu figures

ramen.toppings: Chashu, bamboo shoots, naruto, nori, scallions
ramen.highlight: The archetype of 'Tokyo ramen': clear soy broth and a slice of naruto — the taste of the Shōwa era

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: brewed from the underground waters of the Okutama gorge — a rare Tokyo sake

sengoku_daimyo: Miura clan (Arai Castle, destroyed by the Hōjō in 1516)

meiji_transition.summary: Kanagawa-fu became Kanagawa Prefecture in 1868; the Sagami part of Ashigara Prefecture joined in 1876, and the three Tama districts went to Tokyo in 1893.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Kanagawa is all of Sagami plus southern Musashi — Yokohama and Kawasaki are really 'Musashi', not 'Sagami'.

history_timeline.title: Warriors of Sagami
history_timeline.summary: In the late Heian period Bandō warriors such as the Miura and Ōba rose in Sagami, laying the groundwork for Minamoto no Yoritomo to enter Kamakura in 1180 and found warrior rule.

history_timeline.title: Kamakura, city of the samurai
history_timeline.summary: Yoritomo opened his shogunate and Kamakura became the political center of Japan; Hōjō regent rule lasted over a century, and the Great Buddha of Kamakura was cast in this period.

history_timeline.title: The Kamakura-fu
history_timeline.summary: The Muromachi shogunate set up the Kamakura-fu, where the Kamakura kubō descended from Ashikaga Motouji ruled the Kantō with the Uesugi as kanrei; it declined after the Eikyō War of 1438.

history_timeline.title: Five generations of the Later Hōjō
history_timeline.summary: Ise Sōzui (Hōjō Sōun) seized Odawara and five generations of the Hōjō ruled the Kantō for a century; Odawara Castle surrendered to Hideyoshi's vast army in 1590.

history_timeline.title: The Tōkaidō and the Black Ships
history_timeline.summary: Post towns lined the Tōkaidō; in 1853 Perry's Black Ships arrived at Uraga, and the next year the Japan–US Treaty of Peace and Amity was signed in Yokohama.

history_timeline.title: Yokohama opens
history_timeline.summary: Yokohama opened as a port in 1859, becoming Japan's window on the West; Japan's first railway (Shinbashi–Yokohama) opened in 1872.

landmarks.name: Hakone
landmarks.note: Barrier-station ruins and hot spring towns

specialties.name: Odawara kamaboko
specialties.note: Fish cake made since the Edo period

dialect.name: Kanagawa speech
dialect.features: Largely close to standard Japanese; '-jan' spread nationwide via Yokohama, and western Sagami once used '-be' and '-dabe'.

guide.opening: Meow~ The day the Black Ships came, I was lying on a roof in Uraga! Kanagawa has Kamakura's samurai and Yokohama's foreigners — which side do you want to see first?

regional_meme.title: 'I'm from Yokohama'
regional_meme.text: Yokohama people introduce themselves as 'from Yokohama', never 'from Kanagawa' — much to the annoyance of other Kanagawans.

regional_meme.title: Borders by the sea
regional_meme.text: Shōnan, Yokohama, Kawasaki, Sagami… each goes its own way, and a shared 'Kanagawa identity' is surprisingly thin.

hero_persona.name: Minamoto no Yoritomo
hero_persona.title: Founder of the Kamakura shogunate
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Minamoto no Yoritomo, who founded the house of the warriors at Kamakura. From exile in Izu to head of all the samurai — would you know how I walked that road?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: calm, suspicious and far-sighted; restrained and dignified in speech

ramen.toppings: Chashu, spinach, three sheets of nori
ramen.highlight: Order 'firm noodles, strong flavor, extra oil' — and eat it with a bowl of rice, as is tradition

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: aged pure-rice sake, best served warm

meiji_transition.summary: Niigata and other prefectures were set up in 1871; Kashiwazaki joined in 1873 and Aikawa (Sado) in 1876, and Higashikanbara District came over from Fukushima in 1886, forming today's borders.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Niigata = Echigo + Sado; but Higashikanbara District belonged to the Aizu Domain (Iwashiro) and moved from Fukushima only in 1886, so the prefecture reaches a little east of ancient Echigo.

history_timeline.title: Echigo and exile to Sado
history_timeline.summary: The Echigo provincial capital lay near today's Jōetsu; Sado was a place of 'distant exile', receiving Retired Emperor Juntoku, Nichiren and Zeami.

history_timeline.title: Exiles of Sado
history_timeline.summary: Echigo's governors were mostly Hōjō kin; after the Jōkyū War Retired Emperor Juntoku was exiled to Sado, and Nichiren followed in 1271.

history_timeline.title: Echigo Uesugi and the Nagao
history_timeline.summary: The Uesugi held the governorship of Echigo while their deputies, the Nagao, gradually took real power — Uesugi Kenshin was born a Nagao.

history_timeline.title: The Dragon of Echigo
history_timeline.summary: Nagao Kagetora (Uesugi Kenshin) unified Echigo and faced Takeda Shingen five times at Kawanakajima; his successor Kagekatsu was moved to Aizu in 1598.

history_timeline.title: Gold and the Kitamaebune
history_timeline.summary: The Sado gold mine became the shogunate's treasury; Niigata was a key port of call for the Kitamaebune, and the Nagaoka and Shibata domains developed the Echigo Plain.

history_timeline.title: The Hokuetsu Boshin War
history_timeline.summary: Kawai Tsugunosuke of Nagaoka fought the new government with Gatling guns; in the mid-Meiji era Niigata was briefly Japan's most populous prefecture.

landmarks.name: Sado Gold Mine
landmarks.note: Dōyū no Wareto, the split gold vein

specialties.name: Sake
specialties.note: More breweries than any other prefecture

specialties.name: Sasa dango
specialties.note: Mugwort dumplings wrapped in bamboo leaves

dialect.name: Niigata dialect
dialect.features: '-iya' and '-teba' add emphasis and 'dasuke' means 'so'; the Sado dialect keeps a Kansai flavor.

guide.opening: I am Kazama, messenger of the Echigo wind. Lord Kenshin waving his war fan at Kasugayama is still Echigo's pride — shall I report on Kawanakajima, or on the Sado gold mine?

regional_meme.title: Where do we belong?
regional_meme.text: Is Niigata Kantō? Chūbu? Hokuriku? Tōhoku? Weather forecasts, high-school baseball and power companies all disagree — even locals can't say.

regional_meme.title: Rice and sake
regional_meme.text: Niigata people are convinced their Koshihikari and sake are Japan's best; a proper meal starts with white rice.

hero_persona.name: Uesugi Kenshin
hero_persona.title: Dragon of Echigo · avatar of Bishamonten
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Uesugi Kenshin, avatar of Bishamonten. I never fight for personal gain — even when Shingen ran short of salt, I let it through. Shall I tell you of Kawanakajima?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: lofty and righteous with an otherworldly air; terse and solemn, often speaking of 'righteousness'

ramen.toppings: Diced onion, chashu, lots of back fat
ramen.highlight: Invented so craftsmen's deliveries wouldn't go soggy or cold — the back fat covers the soup like snow

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: the very symbol of 'tanrei karakuchi', clean and sharp

meiji_transition.summary: Toyama Prefecture, set up in 1871, was renamed Niikawa, merged into Ishikawa in 1876 and re-established as Toyama in 1883.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Toyama ≈ Etchū Province; but in the Edo period most of Etchū was ruled directly by the Kaga Domain, with only the area around Toyama a branch domain — Etchū long answered to Kanazawa.

history_timeline.title: Ōtomo no Yakamochi in Etchū
history_timeline.summary: Appointed governor of Etchū in 746, Ōtomo no Yakamochi wrote over 200 Man'yōshū poems here; the provincial office stood at Fushiki in today's Takaoka.

history_timeline.title: Etchū under the Hōjō
history_timeline.summary: Etchū's governors were mostly the Nagoe branch of the Hōjō; the 1183 Battle of Kurikara Pass had already secured Minamoto dominance in Hokuriku.

history_timeline.title: The Hatakeyama and the Ikkō sect
history_timeline.summary: The Hatakeyama, one of the three kanrei houses, held Etchū while deputies like the Jinbo and Shiina ruled in practice; after Rennyo's preaching the Ikkō sect took root in Tonami.

history_timeline.title: Sassa Narimasa's snow crossing
history_timeline.summary: Sassa Narimasa held Toyama Castle against Hideyoshi and, legend says, crossed the Tateyama range in midwinter (the 'Sara-sara-goe') to seek Ieyasu's help — but in the end he submitted.

history_timeline.title: Etchū medicine peddlers
history_timeline.summary: Maeda Masatoshi, second lord of Toyama, promoted the medicine 'Hangontan'; under the 'use first, pay later' system Toyama's peddlers traveled all over Japan.

history_timeline.title: Hydropower and aluminum
history_timeline.summary: Toyama broke away from Ishikawa in 1883; hydropower on the Kurobe River (Kurobe Dam, 1963) fed heavy industries such as aluminum.

landmarks.name: Takaoka Great Buddha
landmarks.note: One of Japan's three great Buddhas

specialties.name: Masu-zushi
specialties.note: Pressed trout sushi in bamboo leaves

specialties.name: Firefly squid
specialties.note: Tiny squid that glow on spring nights

dialect.name: Toyama dialect
dialect.features: Sentences end in '-cha' and '-gaize'; 'kitokito' — fresh and lively — is a local trademark word.

guide.opening: I am Kazama, just over the snow walls of Tateyama. Sassa Narimasa crossed here too, they say… though he did it in the dead of winter. Shall I tell you the legend?

regional_meme.title: Hokuriku ranking wars
regional_meme.text: In what order do the three Hokuriku prefectures go? Toyama says 'Toyama, Ishikawa, Fukui'; Ishikawa says 'Ishikawa, Toyama, Fukui'…

regional_meme.title: Savings and big houses
regional_meme.text: Toyama people are known for high home ownership, big houses and big savings — 'Japan's thriftiest prefecture'.

hero_persona.name: Sassa Narimasa
hero_persona.title: The general who crossed Tateyama in the snow
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Sassa Narimasa. To urge Lord Ieyasu to keep fighting Hideyoshi, I crossed the Tateyama range in midwinter — can you understand such stubbornness?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: obstinate and fiery, refuses to give in; bitter whenever Hideyoshi comes up

ramen.toppings: Coarse black pepper, scallions, bamboo shoots, chashu
ramen.highlight: Pitch-black and astonishingly salty — originally a 'rice-companion soup' for manual laborers

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: crisp and clean, great with Toyama Bay fish

sengoku_daimyo: Kaga Ikkō uprising ('the province held by the peasants')

meiji_transition.summary: Kanazawa Prefecture was renamed Ishikawa in 1872; in 1876 it absorbed Etchū and northern Echizen, but Echizen left in 1881 and Etchū in 1883, returning it to Kaga plus Noto.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: From 1876 to 1881 'Greater Ishikawa' spanned four provinces — Kaga, Noto, Etchū and Echizen — one of the most populous prefectures of early Meiji.

history_timeline.title: Kaga splits off
history_timeline.summary: Noto was split from Echizen in 718 and Kaga in 823 — the last ritsuryō province ever created.

history_timeline.title: The Togashi and Noto
history_timeline.summary: Local warriors such as the Togashi of Kaga were granted land; Noto's governors were mostly Hōjō kin.

history_timeline.title: The Togashi and Rennyo
history_timeline.summary: The Togashi held Kaga; in the late Muromachi period Rennyo preached at Yoshizaki in Echizen and Kaga's believers multiplied — the seeds of the later 'province of the peasants'.

history_timeline.title: Province held by the peasants
history_timeline.summary: In 1488 the Ikkō uprising overthrew the governor Togashi Masachika, and Kaga was self-governed by Hongan-ji believers for nearly a century until Shibata Katsuie subdued it in 1580.

history_timeline.title: Kaga, a million koku
history_timeline.summary: The Maeda, largest of the outer lords, deliberately poured money into arts and crafts to allay shogunal suspicion, making Kanazawa a 'little Kyoto'.

history_timeline.title: City of crafts
history_timeline.summary: Kutani ware, gold leaf and Kaga yūzen live on; the Hokuriku Shinkansen reached Kanazawa in 2015, and the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake caused severe damage.

landmarks.name: Kenroku-en
landmarks.note: One of Japan's three great gardens

landmarks.name: Shiroyone Senmaida
landmarks.note: Seaside terraced rice fields of Noto

dialect.name: Kanazawa dialect
dialect.features: The polite invitation '-masshi' is well known; its strong rises and falls are called the lilting Hokuriku accent.

phrases.meaning: thank you, sorry to trouble you

guide.opening: I am Kazama, sent to infiltrate Kanazawa Castle… just kidding. Did you know Kaga was ruled by its peasants for nearly a century, long before the Maeda's million koku?

regional_meme.title: Little Kyoto rivalry
regional_meme.text: Kanazawa calls itself a 'little Kyoto', which Kyoto doesn't quite accept — and Kanazawa would rather just be Kanazawa anyway.

regional_meme.title: Thunder and yellowtail
regional_meme.text: Yellowtail is fattest when winter thunder rolls; Hokuriku people call that thunder 'buri-okoshi' — the yellowtail wake-up call.

hero_persona.name: Maeda Toshiie
hero_persona.title: Founder of Kaga's million koku · 'Mataza of the spear'
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Maeda Matazaemon Toshiie! In my youth I was a notorious kabukimono; later I became lord of Kaga's million koku — what can I do for you?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: hearty and loyal, with traces of his wild youth; deeply respectful of his wife Matsu

ramen.toppings: Heaps of stir-fried vegetables, naruto stamped with an '8'
ramen.highlight: Born at a chain shop on Route 8 — the naruto in the bowl carries an '8'

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: yamahai-brewed, heavy and full

meiji_transition.summary: Fukui and other prefectures were set up in 1871; in 1876 Echizen joined Ishikawa and Wakasa joined Shiga, and in 1881 the two were reunited as Fukui.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Reihoku (Echizen) and Reinan (Wakasa) are divided by the Kinome Pass and differ in speech and culture: Reinan leans toward Kyoto, Reihoku toward Hokuriku.

history_timeline.title: The Koshi provinces split
history_timeline.summary: Ancient Koshi was split in the late 7th century into Echizen, Etchū and Echigo; Wakasa, a 'miketsukuni', supplied seafood to the court.

history_timeline.title: Founding of Eihei-ji
history_timeline.summary: In 1244 Dōgen founded Eihei-ji in Echizen, where the Sōtō school took root.

history_timeline.title: The Shiba and the Asakura
history_timeline.summary: Echizen's governors were the Shiba, one of the three kanrei houses, while their deputies the Asakura grew stronger; during the Ōnin War Asakura Takakage seized Echizen.

history_timeline.title: Asakura of Ichijōdani
history_timeline.summary: Five generations of the Asakura built a thriving castle town at Ichijōdani, destroyed by Oda Nobunaga in 1573; Shibata Katsuie then built Kitanoshō Castle.

history_timeline.title: The Echizen Matsudaira
history_timeline.summary: Yūki Hideyasu, Ieyasu's second son, was given Echizen and founded the Fukui Domain; in the late Edo period its lord Matsudaira Shungaku promoted Hashimoto Sanai and Yuri Kimimasa.

history_timeline.title: Eyeglasses and dinosaurs
history_timeline.summary: From late Meiji an eyeglass-frame industry grew (Sabae makes about 90% of Japan's frames), and Katsuyama has yielded a wealth of dinosaur fossils.

landmarks.name: Eihei-ji
landmarks.note: Head temple of the Sōtō school

specialties.name: Wakasa-nuri chopsticks
specialties.note: Lacquered with shell and gold leaf

dialect.name: Fukui dialect
dialect.features: Reihoku speech has a distinctive rise and fall, ending in '-za' or '-no'; 'hoyahoya' means 'yes, yes'.

guide.opening: I am Kazama, just out of the Ichijōdani ruins. The Asakura castle town was once the 'little Kyoto' of Hokuriku — burned to the ground by Nobunaga overnight. Shall I tell you?

regional_meme.title: Where is Fukui?
regional_meme.text: Fukui is often mistaken for Fukuoka or Fukushima; locals are used to saying 'It's Fukui! Glasses and dinosaurs!'

regional_meme.title: Happiest in Japan
regional_meme.text: Little known, yet Fukui tops the 'happiness ranking' year after year — locals say keeping a low profile is its own blessing.

hero_persona.name: Shibata Katsuie
hero_persona.title: 'Demon Shibata' · chief retainer of the Oda
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Shibata Katsuie, called 'Demon Shibata'! I guard Echizen from Kitanoshō Castle — and you'd best not mention that monkey Hideyoshi.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: fierce and blunt, loyal to a fault, more careful than he looks; utterly devoted to Nobunaga

ramen.highlight: Late-night ramen born at the street stalls in front of Tsuruga Station

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: a pioneer of daiginjō, elegant and delicate

meiji_transition.summary: Kōfu Prefecture was created in 1871 and renamed Yamanashi the same year.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Yamanashi exactly matches Kai Province — a basin ringed by mountains whose borders haven't moved in a thousand years. The name comes from the ancient 'Yamanashi District'.

history_timeline.title: The black horses of Kai
history_timeline.summary: Kai was famous for its 'black horses of Kai', raised on imperial pastures for the court.

history_timeline.title: The Kai Genji Takeda
history_timeline.summary: Takeda Nobuyoshi of the Kai Genji fought in the Genpei War and the Takeda became governors of Kai; in 1274 Nichiren founded Kuon-ji on Mount Minobu.

history_timeline.title: The Uesugi Zenshū Rebellion
history_timeline.summary: In the 1416 Uesugi Zenshū Rebellion Takeda Nobumitsu was killed, leaving Kai without a governor and splintered among local lords.

history_timeline.title: Takeda Shingen
history_timeline.summary: Takeda Shingen, who said 'people are the castle, people are the wall', built the Shingen levee and issued Kōshū gold and a house code; his son Katsuyori was destroyed in 1582.

history_timeline.title: Shogunal Kōfu
