history_timeline.summary: Kai became a bastion guarding Edo's west, ruled for a time by Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu and later directly by the shogunate under the Kōfu Kinban.

history_timeline.title: Grapes and Fuji
history_timeline.summary: Wine and crystal crafts developed in the Meiji era; tourism boomed at the Fuji Five Lakes on Mount Fuji's north slope.

specialties.name: Hōtō
specialties.note: Flat noodles stewed with pumpkin in miso

specialties.name: Shingen mochi
specialties.note: Mochi with kinako and black syrup

dialect.name: Kōshū dialect
dialect.features: Endings like '-zura', '-jan' and '-ke'; 'Te!' as an exclamation of surprise is distinctive.

guide.opening: I am Kazama, once a spy under Lord Shingen's 'Mitsumono'. Under the banner of Fūrinkazan, every mountain in Kai is a castle wall — shall I tell you of the Shingen levee?

regional_meme.title: Who owns Mount Fuji?
regional_meme.text: Does Mount Fuji belong to Yamanashi or Shizuoka? The two argue endlessly — and above the eighth station there's still no prefectural border at all!

regional_meme.title: No sea, but…
regional_meme.text: Landlocked Yamanashi is one of Japan's biggest tuna-eating prefectures.

hero_persona.name: Takeda Shingen
hero_persona.title: Tiger of Kai · Fūrinkazan
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Takeda Shingen. Swift as the wind, silent as the forest, fierce as fire, immovable as the mountain — people are the castle, people are the wall. Will you ask of war, or of governing?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: calm and dignified, uses metaphors to explain strategy and flood control; speaks of his rival Kenshin with respect

ramen.highlight: Yamanashi's noodle stars are hōtō and Yoshida udon; ramen here is a simple chūka soba

sake.taste_profile: Light & sweet: brewed with Southern Alps spring water, soft and smooth

meiji_transition.summary: In 1871 northern Shinano became Nagano Prefecture while central and southern Shinano plus Hida became Chikuma Prefecture; Chikuma's Shinano part joined Nagano in 1876.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Nagano ≈ Shinano; but the north and the central-south long feuded, even sparking a movement to split the prefecture — the prefectural song 'Shinano no Kuni' is what holds everyone together.

history_timeline.title: The Shinano provincial capital
history_timeline.summary: The Shinano provincial capital later moved to Matsumoto (Chikuma District); Zenkō-ji, said to date from the 7th century, became a nationwide center of faith.

history_timeline.title: Shinano and the Nakasendai Rebellion
history_timeline.summary: Shinano's governors were mostly Hōjō kin and the Suwa were Hōjō retainers; in 1335 the Suwa rallied behind Hōjō Tokiyuki in the Nakasendai Rebellion.

history_timeline.title: The Battle of Ōtō
history_timeline.summary: The Ogasawara held Shinano, but local lords like the Murakami, Suwa and Takanashi were strong; at the 1400 Battle of Ōtō the governor was beaten by their alliance.

history_timeline.title: Kawanakajima
history_timeline.summary: Takeda Shingen conquered most of Shinano and fought Uesugi Kenshin five times at Kawanakajima; Sanada Masayuki twice repelled the Tokugawa at Ueda Castle.

history_timeline.title: The Kiso road of the Nakasendō
history_timeline.summary: The Nakasendō ran through the Kiso Valley, where Tsumago and Narai thrived; the Sanada held Matsushiro until the end of the Edo period, and Sakuma Shōzan came from there.

history_timeline.title: Winter Olympics prefecture
history_timeline.summary: Okaya's silk industry once earned Japan's foreign currency; Nagano hosted the 1998 Winter Olympics.

landmarks.name: Kamikōchi
landmarks.note: Kappa Bridge in the Northern Alps

dialect.name: Shinshū dialect
dialect.features: 'Zuku' (get-up-and-go) is the signature word, with endings like '-zura' and '-dani'; the north, center and south differ quite a bit.

guide.opening: I am Kazama, hurrying here from the Sanada's Ueda Castle. Shinano was the fiercest mountain battleground of the Sengoku era — the mist over Kawanakajima hasn't lifted yet. Which battle shall I report?

regional_meme.title: Capital wars and the prefectural song
regional_meme.text: Nagano and Matsumoto fought over the prefectural capital for a century; the cure is the prefectural song 'Shinano no Kuni', which nearly everyone in Nagano can sing.

regional_meme.title: Education prefecture
regional_meme.text: Shinshū people pride themselves on valuing education — 'Shinshū kyōiku' is a badge of honor.

hero_persona.name: Sanada Yukimura
hero_persona.title: 'The finest warrior in Japan'
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Sanada Saemonnosuke Nobushige, though people call me Yukimura. At the Summer Siege of Osaka I charged straight at Ieyasu's headquarters — the six coins are the fare across the river of death.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: loyal and brave, unafraid of death; proud when speaking of his father Masayuki and Ueda Castle

ramen.highlight: Seasoned with local Shinshū miso — milder than Sapporo's

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: birthplace of 'Yeast No. 7', the benchmark of Shinshū sake

meiji_transition.summary: In 1871 Mino became Gifu Prefecture while Hida belonged to Chikuma Prefecture; Hida joined Gifu in 1876.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Mino (plains) and Hida (mountains) differ greatly in culture; locals still distinguish 'Gifu' from 'Hida'.

history_timeline.title: The Fuwa Barrier
history_timeline.summary: The Fuwa Barrier on the Tōsandō was one of the three ancient barriers — the 'seki' in 'Kantō' and 'Kansai' originally meant barriers like this.

history_timeline.title: The Toki of Mino
history_timeline.summary: The Seiwa Genji Toki took root in Mino; in the 1221 Jōkyū War the Mino–Owari area became a battleground between the court and the shogunate.

history_timeline.title: The Toki at their height
history_timeline.summary: Toki Yoriyasu was at one point governor of Mino, Owari and Ise; despite the Toki Yasuyuki Rebellion the Toki kept Mino, while their deputies the Saitō grew stronger.

history_timeline.title: Tenka Fubu
history_timeline.summary: Saitō Dōsan, 'the Viper of Mino', rose from below; in 1567 Oda Nobunaga took Inabayama Castle, renamed it Gifu and began using his 'Tenka Fubu' seal. Sekigahara (1600) was fought here too.

history_timeline.title: Shogunal Hida
history_timeline.summary: Hida was put under direct shogunal rule for its timber and minerals; Takayama Jin'ya is the only surviving intendant's office. Mino was a patchwork of small domains and shogunal land.

history_timeline.title: Shirakawa-gō
history_timeline.summary: The gasshō villages of Shirakawa-gō became World Heritage in 1995; Seki cutlery and Mino washi carry old traditions forward.

dialect.name: Mino and Hida dialects
dialect.features: Mino speech is close to Nagoya's, ending in '-yao' or '-yamon'; Hida speech uses '-yasa'.

guide.opening: I am Kazama. From atop Gifu Castle, Lord Nobunaga once looked out over the whole Nōbi Plain and inscribed the words 'Tenka Fubu' here. Shall I tell you?

regional_meme.title: Nagoya's back garden
regional_meme.text: People in southern Gifu say they're 'going to Nagoya' so often they're teased as 'Gifu-prefecture Nagoyans'.

regional_meme.title: Shirakawa-gō is too famous
regional_meme.text: Foreign tourists know Shirakawa-gō but have no idea it's in Gifu.

hero_persona.name: Saitō Dōsan
hero_persona.title: The Viper of Mino
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Saitō Dōsan. From oil merchant to lord of Mino — they call me 'the Viper'. Hmph, in an age of chaos, what's wrong with rising from below?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: shrewd and cunning with a warlord's air, yet full of praise for his son-in-law Nobunaga's talent

ramen.broth: Shōyu (chicken and bonito; tare boiled with the stock)
ramen.highlight: Locals call it 'chūka soba' — simmering the tare together with the stock is unique

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: a Mino sake famed for being 'ultra-dry'

meiji_transition.summary: In 1868 the Tokugawa main house was moved to Sunpu (Shizuoka Domain), which became Shizuoka Prefecture in 1871; Hamamatsu Prefecture (Tōtōmi) and the Izu part of Ashigara Prefecture joined in 1876.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Shizuoka was stitched from three provinces — Izu in the east, Suruga in the center, Tōtōmi in the west — about 155 km end to end, and the three still differ in dialect and daily life.

history_timeline.title: Three provinces side by side
history_timeline.summary: Tōtōmi, Suruga and Izu lined the Tōkaidō; 'Tōtōmi' means 'the distant freshwater lake' (Lake Hamana), as opposed to 'Ōmi' (Lake Biwa).

history_timeline.title: The Hōjō of Izu
history_timeline.summary: The Hōjō came from Hōjō in Izu; Minamoto no Yoritomo rose from his exile in Izu, and in 1193 held the great 'Fuji no Makigari' hunt at the foot of Mount Fuji.

history_timeline.title: The Imagawa of Suruga
history_timeline.summary: The Imagawa, an Ashikaga branch, held Suruga for generations; men like Imagawa Ryōshun excelled in letters and arms, and Sunpu became a key hub of the Tōkai.

history_timeline.title: Imagawa and Ieyasu
history_timeline.summary: Imagawa Yoshimoto, 'the best bowman of the Tōkaidō', fell at Okehazama in 1560; Tokugawa Ieyasu, based at Hamamatsu, was badly beaten by Takeda Shingen at Mikatagahara in 1572.

history_timeline.title: The retired shogun at Sunpu
history_timeline.summary: After stepping down Ieyasu retired to Sunpu and steered the early shogunate; 22 Tōkaidō post towns lay here, and the Hakone and Arai barriers checked travelers.

history_timeline.title: Tea and the Tokugawa
history_timeline.summary: Tokugawa Yoshinobu retired to Shizuoka and former shogunal retainers cleared the Makinohara tea fields; Shizuoka tea now leads Japan, and Yamaha and Suzuki began in Hamamatsu.

specialties.name: Sakura shrimp
specialties.note: Pink shrimp found only in Suruga Bay

dialect.name: Shizuoka dialect
dialect.features: '-dara', '-zura' and '-dani'; Enshū's 'yaramaika!' (let's do it!) sums up Hamamatsu's pioneering spirit.

phrases.meaning: Let's do it! Let's give it a go!

guide.opening: I am Kazama. Lord Ieyasu said, 'Life is a long journey with a heavy load — do not hurry.' He spent his last years here at Sunpu Castle. Shall I tell you of that crushing defeat at Mikatagahara?

regional_meme.title: Who owns Mount Fuji?
regional_meme.text: Shizuoka: 'Mount Fuji is ours!' The argument with Yamanashi never ends — and there's still no border near the summit.

regional_meme.title: Too long east to west
regional_meme.text: Eastern Shizuoka sounds like Kantō, the west like Nagoya — people at either end think the other side is 'from another prefecture'.

hero_persona.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
hero_persona.title: Tōshō Daigongen · retired shogun of Sunpu
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Tokugawa Ieyasu. Life is a long journey with a heavy load — do not hurry. I spent my last years at Sunpu. Would you ask how I endured to the very end?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: calm, patient and far-sighted; speaks slowly and often counsels endurance

ramen.highlight: Tea farmers eat it after early-morning work: one hot bowl and one cold bowl of 'morning ramen'

sake.taste_profile: Light & sweet: the crisp fruity aroma typical of Shizuoka ginjō

meiji_transition.summary: In 1871 Owari became Nagoya Prefecture and Mikawa became Nukata Prefecture; Nagoya was renamed Aichi in 1872 and absorbed Nukata the same year.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Owari and Mikawa are divided by the Sakai River and differ in dialect and temperament — people still speak of 'Owari vs. Mikawa'.

history_timeline.title: Atsuta and Mikawa
history_timeline.summary: Atsuta Shrine enshrines Kusanagi, one of the three sacred treasures; the Mikawa provincial capital lay in today's Toyokawa.

history_timeline.title: Atsuta and the Jōkyū War
history_timeline.summary: Minamoto no Yoritomo's mother was a daughter of the Atsuta chief priest; in the Jōkyū War the Owari (Kiso) River area became a battleground between the shogunate and the court.

history_timeline.title: Shiba and Isshiki
history_timeline.summary: Owari's governors were the Shiba, one of the three kanrei houses, with their deputies the Oda ruling in practice; Mikawa was held by the Isshiki and others while the Matsudaira rose in the Mikawa hills.

history_timeline.title: The three unifiers
history_timeline.summary: Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi were born in Owari and Tokugawa Ieyasu at Okazaki in Mikawa — all three Sengoku unifiers came from here, and Okehazama and Nagashino were fought within the prefecture.

history_timeline.title: Owari, a Gosanke house
history_timeline.summary: Ieyasu's son Yoshinao was given Owari; Nagoya Castle was built from 1610, and the whole town of Kiyosu was moved ('Kiyosu-goshi') to create Nagoya.

history_timeline.title: Industrial heart
history_timeline.summary: Toyota and other manufacturers made Aichi Japan's top manufacturing prefecture; it hosted Expo 2005.

landmarks.name: Atsuta Shrine
landmarks.note: Shrine of the sacred sword Kusanagi

specialties.name: Miso katsu
specialties.note: Pork cutlet with Hatchō miso sauce

specialties.name: Hitsumabushi
specialties.note: Nagoya-style eel over rice, eaten three ways

dialect.name: Nagoya dialect
dialect.features: Vowels merge (ai → ææ, as in '-dagyaa'); 'dera' means very, and a bicycle is a 'kettā mashīn'.

guide.opening: I am Kazama. Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu all grew up drinking this water — shall I report on the surprise attack at Okehazama, or on Nagoya Castle's golden shachihoko?

regional_meme.title: Boring Nagoya?
regional_meme.text: One survey named Nagoya 'the most boring city' — Nagoya struck back with 'Nagoya meshi', where everything gets miso.

regional_meme.title: Three-unifier pride
regional_meme.text: Aichi people on Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu: 'The whole realm was won by people from here.'

hero_persona.name: Oda Nobunaga
hero_persona.title: The Demon King of the Sixth Heaven
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Oda Kazusanosuke Nobunaga! Fifty years of human life, set against the heavens, are but a dream — if it's 'Tenka Fubu' you want to ask about, speak up.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: commanding and decisive, terse, with an innovator's arrogance; disdains old custom

ramen.toppings: Spicy stir-fried minced pork, garlic chives, garlic
ramen.highlight: A Nagoya original — there's no 'Taiwan ramen' in Taiwan

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: bright sweet-tart notes, found in Paris's starred restaurants

edo_domains: Tsu Domain (Tōdō clan, also ruling Iga)

meiji_transition.summary: In 1871 Anotsu Prefecture (north) and Watarai Prefecture (south) were set up; Anotsu was renamed Mie in 1872 and Watarai joined in 1876.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Mie spans four provinces — Ise, Iga, Shima and eastern Kii; the Kumano area belonged to Kii and shares roots with Wakayama, so the Kumano Kodō crosses both prefectures.

history_timeline.title: The Grand Shrine and the Saikū
history_timeline.summary: Ise Grand Shrine enshrines Amaterasu, the imperial ancestor, and the court sent an imperial princess to live at the Saikū as high priestess; Shima was a 'miketsukuni'.

history_timeline.title: Ise Shintō
history_timeline.summary: After the Genpei War Ise, old Taira country, came under the shogunate; the Watarai family of the Outer Shrine developed 'Ise Shintō'.

history_timeline.title: The Kitabatake governors
history_timeline.summary: The Kitabatake, key Southern Court vassals, ruled southern Ise as provincial governors from Taki, lasting into the Sengoku period.

history_timeline.title: Ninja of Iga
history_timeline.summary: The samurai of Iga governed themselves as the 'Sōkoku Ikki' until crushed by the Oda in the 1581 Tenshō Iga War; Kuki Yoshitaka's iron-clad ships defeated the Mōri navy.

history_timeline.title: The Ise pilgrimage
history_timeline.summary: 'Once in a lifetime to Ise' became a common dream, with millions flocking there in 'okage-mairi' waves; Matsusaka merchants (the Mitsui) rose to prominence.

history_timeline.title: Pearls and industry
history_timeline.summary: Mikimoto Kōkichi succeeded in culturing pearls at Toba; the Yokkaichi petrochemical complex also caused 'Yokkaichi asthma' pollution.

landmarks.name: Meoto Iwa
landmarks.note: Wedded rocks joined by a sacred rope at Futami

specialties.name: Matsusaka beef
specialties.note: One of Japan's three great wagyu

specialties.name: Akafuku mochi
specialties.note: Red-bean mochi of the Ise pilgrimage

dialect.name: Ise dialect
dialect.features: Mostly Kansai-style, ending in '-yanka' or '-damonde'; Iga speech is closer to Kyoto's.

guide.opening: I once traveled to Ise at the High Priestess's command… a thousand years ago now. The pilgrims still crowd to Ise today — shall I tell you of the Saikū, or of the Iga ninja?

regional_meme.title: Kansai or Tōkai?
regional_meme.text: Is Mie part of Kansai or Tōkai? Weather, high-school baseball and TV stations all disagree, and Mie itself is split into two camps.

regional_meme.title: Ise-pilgrimage nonchalance
regional_meme.text: 'Ise Grand Shrine is our local shrine' — Mie people watch the flood of pilgrims with a shrug.

hero_persona.name: Matsuo Bashō
hero_persona.title: Saint of haiku · born in Iga
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Matsuo Bashō, born in Iga-Ueno. Some say I must have been a ninja — how else could I walk so far in a day? Heh — shall I share a haiku?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: relaxed and wry, poetic, occasionally reciting a haiku; the 'Bashō was a ninja' theory is folklore and should be noted as such

ramen.highlight: Mie's noodle star is Ise udon; ramen here is mostly clear-broth chūka soba

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: lively fruit and balanced sweet-tartness — very hard to find

meiji_transition.summary: In 1871 Ōtsu and Nagahama prefectures were created, merging as Shiga in 1872; from 1876 to 1881 Wakasa and Echizen's Tsuruga District were briefly part of Shiga.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Shiga = Ōmi Province. 'Ōmi' means the freshwater lake near the capital (Lake Biwa), as opposed to 'Tōtōmi' (Lake Hamana).

history_timeline.title: Ōmi Ōtsu Palace
history_timeline.summary: Emperor Tenji moved the capital to Ōmi Ōtsu Palace in 667; Saichō founded Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei in 788.

history_timeline.title: The Sasaki of Ōmi
history_timeline.summary: The Uda Genji Sasaki held the governorship of Ōmi; from them came the Rokkaku and Kyōgoku houses.

history_timeline.title: Rokkaku and Kyōgoku
history_timeline.summary: The Rokkaku governed southern Ōmi, the Kyōgoku the north; Sasaki Dōyo of the Kyōgoku was a famous 'basara' lord of the Northern and Southern Courts era.

history_timeline.title: Azuchi Castle
history_timeline.summary: Azai Nagamasa held Odani Castle (Battle of Anegawa, 1570); in 1576 Nobunaga built Azuchi Castle, whose keep set the model for early-modern castles, burned after the Honnō-ji Incident in 1582.

history_timeline.title: Ōmi merchants
history_timeline.summary: The Ii of Hikone led the fudai lords, and the great elder Ii Naosuke signed the commercial treaties; Ōmi merchants, devoted to 'sanpō yoshi' (good for seller, buyer and society), spread across Japan.

history_timeline.title: The Lake Biwa Canal
history_timeline.summary: The 1890 Lake Biwa Canal brought water and hydropower to Kyoto; Lake Biwa supplies about 14.5 million people in Kinki.

landmarks.name: Shirahige Shrine
landmarks.note: A torii standing in Lake Biwa

specialties.name: Ōmi beef
specialties.note: One of Japan's three great wagyu

dialect.name: Ōmi dialect
dialect.features: A Kansai dialect with '-haru' and '-hen' endings, more direct than Kyoto speech; 'hokasu' means to throw away.

guide.opening: I once followed Emperor Tenji's carriage to the Ōmi Ōtsu Palace, and I still remember the shimmer of Lake Biwa. Lord Nobunaga's Azuchi Castle stood by the lake too — which tale would you hear?

regional_meme.title: Kansai water wars
regional_meme.text: A Shiga person's trump card in any argument: 'Keep it up and we'll shut the Lake Biwa sluice gates — no water for Kyoto and Osaka!'

regional_meme.title: Lake Biwa's size
regional_meme.text: Lake Biwa covers about a sixth of Shiga; locals give directions by 'which side of the lake'.

hero_persona.name: Ishida Mitsunari
hero_persona.title: Commander of the Western Army · a man of righteousness
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Ishida Jibu-no-shō Mitsunari, of Ōmi. They say no one liked me — but all I wanted was to protect the late Taikō's realm.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: earnest and rigid, principled and socially awkward, but unwavering in loyalty to the Toyotomi

ramen.toppings: Cabbage, bean sprouts, pork, wood-ear mushrooms
ramen.highlight: Clear golden dashi with heaps of vegetables — add vinegar to change the taste

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: named for the Seven Spears of Shizugatake, mellower with age

sengoku_daimyo: Ashikaga shoguns of the Muromachi shogunate

meiji_transition.summary: Kyoto-fu was established in 1868 and absorbed neighboring prefectures in 1871; in 1876 the five Tango districts and Tanba's Amata District came over from Toyooka Prefecture, giving today's long north–south shape.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Kyoto Prefecture combines Yamashiro (the basin), eastern Tanba and Tango (the Sea of Japan coast) — which is why it stretches from Kyoto city all the way to Amanohashidate.

history_timeline.title: Heian-kyō
history_timeline.summary: In 794 Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō, the imperial seat for the next thousand years; The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book were born here.

history_timeline.title: The Rokuhara Tandai
history_timeline.summary: Power moved east to Kamakura, but Kyoto remained the seat of the court; after the 1221 Jōkyū War the shogunate set up the Rokuhara Tandai to watch over it.

history_timeline.title: Kitayama and Higashiyama cultures
history_timeline.summary: Ashikaga Takauji opened his shogunate in Kyoto; Yoshimitsu built the Golden Pavilion (1397) and Yoshimasa, in his later years, the Silver Pavilion — the Kitayama and Higashiyama cultures in turn.

history_timeline.title: The Ōnin War
history_timeline.summary: The Ōnin War of 1467 reduced Kyoto to ashes and began the Sengoku era; Nobunaga's march on the capital, the Honnō-ji Incident and Hideyoshi's Jurakudai all played out here.

history_timeline.title: City of the emperor
history_timeline.summary: With politics gone east, Kyoto became the city of the emperor, nobles, temples and crafts, where Nishijin weaving and Kyō-yūzen flourished; in the late Edo period loyalists and the Shinsengumi clashed here.

history_timeline.title: The old capital reborn
history_timeline.summary: After the emperor moved east in 1869, Kyoto revived with the Lake Biwa Canal and Japan's first streetcar; its historic monuments became World Heritage in 1994.

landmarks.name: Amanohashidate
landmarks.note: One of the Three Views of Japan

dialect.name: Kyō-kotoba (Kyoto speech)
dialect.features: Soft and indirect, with '-dosu' and '-haru' endings; people speak obliquely — 'Would you like some bubuzuke?' may actually mean 'time to go home'.

phrases.phrase: ぶぶ漬けでもどうどす
phrases.meaning: Would you like some tea over rice?
phrases.note: a polite hint that it's time to leave

guide.opening: I witnessed the great fires of Heian-kyō. Which tale of the past would you like to hear?

regional_meme.title: Kyoto's 'last war'
regional_meme.text: Old Kyotoites are said to mean the Ōnin War (1467) by 'the last war'; the 'bubuzuke' hint to leave is another classic.

regional_meme.title: 'That's not Kyoto'
regional_meme.text: To people in central Kyoto, the north of the prefecture (Tango, Tanba) — and even the city's outskirts — 'aren't really Kyoto'.

hero_persona.name: Akechi Mitsuhide
hero_persona.title: Rebel of the Honnō-ji Incident
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Akechi Hyūga-no-kami Mitsuhide. 'The enemy is at Honnō-ji'… why did I raise my army? Everyone has a theory — would you hear mine?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: refined and somber, cultured; speaks obliquely of the Honnō-ji Incident; note that there is no settled view of his motives

ramen.broth: Shōyu (chicken and pork bone with back fat)
ramen.toppings: Kujō green onion, chashu, back fat
ramen.highlight: Kyotoites actually love rich flavors — both back-fat shōyu and thick chicken paitan were born here

sake.taste_profile: Light & sweet: the soft 'feminine sake' of Fushimi's soft water

meiji_transition.summary: Osaka-fu was set up in 1868; Sakai Prefecture (Izumi, Kawachi, Yamato) joined in 1881, and Yamato split off as Nara in 1887.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Settsu Province is cut in two by the prefectural border — the east belongs to Osaka, the west (Kobe, Amagasaki, Nishinomiya…) to Hyōgo.

history_timeline.title: Naniwa Palace
history_timeline.summary: Naniwa-tsu was the ancient gateway port; Naniwa Nagara-Toyosaki Palace was built after 645, and Daisen Kofun (attributed to Emperor Nintoku) is Japan's largest keyhole tomb.

history_timeline.title: Kusunoki Masashige
history_timeline.summary: Kusunoki Masashige of Kawachi rose for Emperor Go-Daigo, holding off the shogunate's armies with clever tactics at Akasaka and Chihaya castles (1331–33).

history_timeline.title: The Hatakeyama and Sakai
history_timeline.summary: Masashige died at Minatogawa (1336) and his son Masatsura at Shijō-Nawate (1348); Kawachi was later ruled by the Hatakeyama, and Sakai rose as a port for trade with Ming China.

history_timeline.title: Ishiyama Hongan-ji
history_timeline.summary: Ishiyama Hongan-ji, head temple of the Ikkō sect, held out against Nobunaga for ten years (1570–1580); Hideyoshi built Osaka Castle on its site, and the Toyotomi fell in the Summer Siege of 1615.

history_timeline.title: Kitchen of the realm
history_timeline.summary: Osaka became Japan's logistics hub, lined with the domains' warehouses; the Dōjima Rice Exchange saw the world's first futures trading, and townspeople's culture flourished.

history_timeline.title: Greater Osaka
history_timeline.summary: In 1925 Osaka city briefly outnumbered Tokyo — 'Dai-Ōsaka'; it hosted world expos in 1970 and 2025.

dialect.name: Osaka dialect
dialect.features: Fast-paced and full of humor; 'ōkini' (thanks) and 'nande yanen' (why?!) are badges of its comic-retort culture.

guide.opening: Though I lived in Heian-kyō, I often sailed down to Naniwa-tsu. Later Lord Hideyoshi built the realm's greatest castle at Osaka — would you hear of its rise and fall?

regional_meme.title: No retort, no fun
regional_meme.text: In Osaka, a joke with no comeback is the ultimate rudeness — 'nande yanen' is everyday etiquette.

regional_meme.title: Which side of the escalator?
regional_meme.text: Osakans stand on the right of escalators, Tokyoites on the left — a classic Kantō–Kansai rivalry topic.

hero_persona.name: Toyotomi Hideyoshi
hero_persona.title: Unifier of the realm · the Taikō
hero_persona.opening_line: I am the Taikō, Toyotomi Hideyoshi! From a farm boy in Owari to ruler of the realm — and Osaka Castle is my masterpiece, glittering with gold!
hero_persona.tone_prompt: cheerful and outgoing, loves to show off, approachable yet shrewd; full of Osaka-merchant warmth

ramen.highlight: Workers' ramen from Takaida in East Osaka — dark broth, fat noodles

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: home-grown rice, all pure-rice, strongly aged character

meiji_transition.summary: Hyōgo Prefecture (western Settsu) was set up in 1868; in 1876 Shikama Prefecture (Harima), part of Toyooka Prefecture (Tajima and western Tanba) and Awaji from Myōdō Prefecture were added — the 'prefecture of five provinces'.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Hyōgo is the only prefecture spanning five ritsuryō provinces and facing both the Sea of Japan and the Inland Sea; Awaji belonged to the Tokushima Domain and joined Hyōgo only in 1876.

history_timeline.title: Awaji and Fukuhara
history_timeline.summary: Awaji is the first island born in the creation myth; in 1180 Taira no Kiyomori briefly moved the capital to Fukuhara (today's Kobe).

history_timeline.title: Ichi-no-Tani and the vassals
history_timeline.summary: The 1184 Battle of Ichi-no-Tani was fought in western Settsu; in the Kamakura period Harima and other provinces were ruled by eastern warriors such as Kajiwara Kagetoki.

history_timeline.title: Akamatsu and the Kakitsu Incident
history_timeline.summary: Akamatsu Norimura (Enshin) won Harima for his part in toppling the shogunate; in 1441 Akamatsu Mitsusuke assassinated shogun Ashikaga Yoshinori (the Kakitsu Incident), after which the Yamana took over.

history_timeline.title: The Harima campaign
history_timeline.summary: In his western campaign Hideyoshi starved out Miki Castle ('the starving of Miki'); Kuroda Kanbei served as his strategist, and Himeji Castle became the base for subduing the west.

history_timeline.title: The White Heron Castle
history_timeline.summary: Ikeda Terumasa rebuilt Himeji Castle into today's heron-white keep; the Akō Domain's Asano affair — the 'Chūshingura' — became famous nationwide.

history_timeline.title: Kobe opens
history_timeline.summary: Kobe opened as a port in 1868, leaving cosmopolitan traces in the Kitano foreigners' houses and Nankinmachi; the city was rebuilt after the 1995 Great Hanshin–Awaji Earthquake.

landmarks.name: Arima Onsen
landmarks.note: One of Japan's three oldest hot springs

dialect.name: Banshū and Kobe dialects
dialect.features: Banshū speech is famously rough ('dabo' = fool), Kobe speech uses '-tō' for ongoing actions, and Tajima speech is close to Tottori's.

guide.opening: By my count, Hyōgo is stitched from five provinces — Settsu, Harima, Tajima, Tanba and Awaji. How greedy! Shall I begin with the White Heron Castle, or with Taira no Kiyomori's Fukuhara capital?

regional_meme.title: 'I'm from Kobe'
regional_meme.text: Hyōgo people rarely say they're 'from Hyōgo' — they're 'from Kobe' or 'from Himeji'. Five provinces, five identities.

regional_meme.title: A five-province civil war
regional_meme.text: Settsu, Harima, Tajima, Tanba and Awaji are so different that the prefecture is teased as 'five countries holding a UN summit'.

hero_persona.name: Kuroda Kanbei
hero_persona.title: Genius strategist
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Kuroda Kanbei Yoshitaka. I spent a year in the dungeon of Arioka Castle and came out lame — but this head still works fine. What stratagem do you need?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: wise and cool-headed, far-sighted; speaks in questions and step-by-step reasoning

ramen.highlight: A curious hybrid of udon broth and ramen noodles — the standing noodle stall of Himeji Station

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: the 'masculine sake' of Nada's Miyamizu water, the model of kimoto dry sake

meiji_transition.summary: Nara Prefecture was set up in 1871, absorbed into Sakai Prefecture in 1876 and with it into Osaka-fu in 1881, then re-established in 1887.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Nara = Yamato Province; in Meiji it briefly vanished into Osaka-fu and was 'restored' only after years of petitioning by local people.

history_timeline.title: Heijō-kyō
history_timeline.summary: The capital moved to Heijō-kyō in 710 and the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji was consecrated in 752 — the height of the ritsuryō state; Hōryū-ji is the world's oldest surviving group of wooden buildings.

history_timeline.title: Rebuilding Tōdai-ji
history_timeline.summary: After Taira no Shigehira burned Nara in 1180, Chōgen led the rebuilding of Tōdai-ji, and Unkei and Kaikei completed the Kongō Rikishi guardians in 1203.

history_timeline.title: The Southern Court at Yoshino
history_timeline.summary: In 1336 Emperor Go-Daigo fled to Yoshino and founded the Southern Court, beginning over fifty years of rival courts; Kōfuku-ji ruled Nara as governor of Yamato.

history_timeline.title: Warlords of Yamato
history_timeline.summary: Kōfuku-ji long served as Yamato's governor; in 1567 fighting between Matsunaga Hisahide and the Miyoshi Triumvirate burned Tōdai-ji's Great Buddha Hall, and in 1577 Hisahide took his own life at Shigisan Castle.

history_timeline.title: Province of temples
history_timeline.summary: The Kōriyama Domain and the Nara magistrate shared rule; Nara-machi thrived on ink, bleached cloth and Nara-zuke pickles, and Nara's deer were protected.

history_timeline.title: Restoration and heritage
history_timeline.summary: Nara Prefecture was re-established in 1887; Hōryū-ji became World Heritage in 1993 and the monuments of ancient Nara in 1998.

dialect.name: Nara dialect
dialect.features: A Kansai dialect with '-haru' and '-yaru' honorifics; yet around Totsukawa in the south a Tokyo-type accent survives — very rare in Kinki.

phrases.phrase: まんまんちゃん あん
phrases.meaning: pray to the gods and Buddhas (said to children)

guide.opening: When I lived in Heijō-kyō, the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji had only just opened its eyes — the most glorious moment of the ritsuryō state. Would you hear the Great Buddha's story?

regional_meme.title: Nothing good to eat in Nara?
regional_meme.text: 'Nara ni umai mono nashi' — one remark by the writer Shiga Naoya has haunted Nara for a century.

regional_meme.title: More deer than people
regional_meme.text: The deer of Nara Park bow for crackers — and butt you if you don't hand them over.

hero_persona.name: Prince Shōtoku
hero_persona.title: The sage of Asuka
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Prince Umayado, known as Shōtoku Taishi. 'Harmony is to be valued' — the first article of the Seventeen-Article Constitution still lives in Japanese hearts.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: serene and wise, gentle and dignified, speaks of Buddhism and government; legends such as hearing ten people at once should be noted as legends

ramen.toppings: Heaps of spicy stir-fried napa cabbage, garlic chives, pork
ramen.highlight: Spicy cabbage ramen that began at street stalls — Nara's late-night soul food

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: unfiltered, undiluted and lightly fizzy; Nara's Shōryaku-ji is considered the birthplace of refined sake

edo_domains: Shingū Domain (Mizuno clan, senior retainers of Kishū)

meiji_transition.summary: Wakayama Prefecture was set up in 1871, and Tanabe, Shingū and other prefectures joined that year.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Eastern Kii (Kitamuro and Minamimuro in Kumano) went to Mie, so 'Kumano' is split between today's Wakayama and Mie.

history_timeline.title: Kumano and Kōya
history_timeline.summary: Kūkai founded Kongōbu-ji on Mount Kōya in 816; the Three Grand Shrines of Kumano became the sacred goal of retired emperors and nobles on the 'Kumano pilgrimage'.

history_timeline.title: Mount Kōya and Kumano
history_timeline.summary: The Kumano pilgrimage stayed popular in the Kamakura period, and Mount Kōya's temple lands grew into a major power in Kii.

history_timeline.title: The Hatakeyama and Negoro-ji
history_timeline.summary: Kii's governors were the Hatakeyama; Negoro-ji's warrior monks grew powerful — the origin of the later musket mercenaries.

history_timeline.title: Saika and Negoro
history_timeline.summary: The Saika and Negoro bands, famed musket mercenaries, fought Nobunaga in the Ishiyama war; Hideyoshi subdued the region in his 1585 Kishū campaign.

history_timeline.title: The Kishū Tokugawa
history_timeline.summary: Ieyasu's tenth son Yorinobu was given Kishū; its fifth lord Yoshimune later became the eighth shogun and carried out the Kyōhō Reforms.

history_timeline.title: Minakata Kumagusu
history_timeline.summary: The naturalist Minakata Kumagusu was born here; the 'Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range' became World Heritage in 2004.

dialect.name: Wakayama dialect
dialect.features: 'Z' sounds often become 'd' ('zenzen' → 'denden'), honorifics are almost absent, and '-yoshi' and '-ra' are common.

guide.opening: I once walked the Kumano Kodō on a retired emperor's pilgrimage — a mountain road of more than twenty days. Shall I tell of the Three Grand Shrines of Kumano, or of Shogun Yoshimune's origins?

regional_meme.title: The forgotten Kansai
regional_meme.text: Say 'Kansai' and people think Kyoto, Osaka, Kobe… Wakayama: 'And us!'

regional_meme.title: Panda country
regional_meme.text: Adventure World in Shirahama has raised many giant pandas — Wakayama considers itself Japan's panda homeland.

hero_persona.name: Tokugawa Yoshimune
hero_persona.title: The 'Abarenbō Shōgun' · Kyōhō Reforms
hero_persona.opening_line: I am the eighth shogun, Tokugawa Yoshimune, of Kishū. On TV I ride a white horse in disguise punishing villains — that's fiction! The Kyōhō Reforms, though, were real.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: practical and robust, approachable; keen on thrift, new rice fields and lifting the ban on Western books

ramen.highlight: Mackerel 'haya-zushi' sits on every table — ramen with sushi is the local rule

sake.taste_profile: Light & sweet: fresh fruity aroma, the signature of a young brewer

meiji_transition.summary: Tottori Prefecture was set up in 1871, merged into Shimane in 1876 and split off again in 1881.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Tottori = Inaba (east) + Hōki (west); it was swallowed by Shimane for five years and re-established because people resented having their prefectural office far away in Matsue.

history_timeline.title: The White Hare of Inaba
history_timeline.summary: Setting of the Kojiki tale of the White Hare of Inaba; Ōtomo no Yakamochi, governor of Inaba, wrote the very last poem of the Man'yōshū here.

history_timeline.title: The emperor on Mount Senjō
history_timeline.summary: In 1333 Nawa Nagatoshi welcomed Emperor Go-Daigo, escaped from Oki, at Mount Senjō in Hōki and helped him overthrow the shogunate.

history_timeline.title: Yamana, 'lord of a sixth'
history_timeline.summary: The Yamana held Inaba, Hōki and other San'in provinces — at their height they were called 'Rokubun-no-ichi-dono', lords of a sixth of the realm.

history_timeline.title: The starvation of Tottori
history_timeline.summary: In 1581 Hideyoshi starved out Tottori Castle; its commander Kikkawa Tsuneie took his own life to spare the lives of his men and surrendered the castle.

history_timeline.title: Ikeda, 320,000 koku
history_timeline.summary: Ikeda Mitsunaka was given Tottori, and the Ikeda ruled Inaba and Hōki until the end of the Edo period.

history_timeline.title: Restored prefecture and dunes
history_timeline.summary: Tottori was restored in 1881; it is Japan's least populous prefecture, and the Tottori Sand Dunes and 'Kitarō Road' are its calling cards.

landmarks.name: Sanbutsu-ji Nageiredō
landmarks.note: A national-treasure hall perched on a cliff

specialties.name: Matsuba crab
specialties.note: Winter snow crab of the San'in coast

dialect.name: Tottori dialect
dialect.features: Inaba speech differs from Hōki speech (close to Izumo's); 'darazu' means fool, with endings like '-dakee'.

guide.opening: This old man is a kataribe of Izumo, a teller of ancient tales. This is where the White Hare met the god Ōkuninushi in the Kojiki — and later, where Hideyoshi starved a castle into surrender…

regional_meme.title: No Starbucks, but dunes
regional_meme.text: Tottori was once the only prefecture without a Starbucks; its governor quipped, 'We don't have Sutaba, but we have Sunaba (the sand pit)!'

regional_meme.title: Tottori or Shimane?
regional_meme.text: Outsiders can never remember which of Tottori and Shimane is on the left — the answer: Tottori is on the right (east).

hero_persona.name: Kikkawa Tsuneie
hero_persona.title: The commander who died to save his garrison
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Kikkawa Tsuneie. Tottori Castle was surrounded and its food ran out… I traded my life for the lives of thousands of my soldiers, and I do not regret it.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: solemn and quiet, with a strong sense of duty; grave when speaking of the siege

ramen.highlight: A rare beef-bone broth, sweet with the aroma of beef fat

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: brewed with Daisen spring water, best served warm

meiji_transition.summary: Shimane and other prefectures were set up in 1871; in 1876 Hamada Prefecture (Iwami) joined and Tottori was absorbed, but Tottori split off again in 1881.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Shimane = Izumo + Iwami + Oki. Eastern Izumo and western Iwami differ sharply: Izumo's dialect resembles the 'zūzū-ben' of Tōhoku, while Iwami's is close to Hiroshima's.

history_timeline.title: Izumo mythology
history_timeline.summary: Izumo Taisha enshrines the god Ōkuninushi, and the Izumo Fudoki is the only gazetteer to survive almost intact; every tenth lunar month the gods gather here, so Izumo calls it 'the month with gods'.

history_timeline.title: Retired emperors on Oki
history_timeline.summary: After the Jōkyū War Retired Emperor Go-Toba was exiled to Oki until his death; Emperor Go-Daigo was exiled there too in 1332, escaping the next year.

history_timeline.title: The Kyōgoku and the Amago
history_timeline.summary: Izumo's governors were the Kyōgoku, whose deputies the Amago grew ever stronger; Iwami was held by the Ōuchi and the Masuda.

history_timeline.title: Amago and Mōri
history_timeline.summary: Amago Tsunehisa, 'the master schemer', unified the San'in; in 1566 Gassan-Toda Castle fell to Mōri Motonari, and Yamanaka Shikanosuke vowed to restore the Amago — 'Grant me the seven hardships and eight sufferings'.

history_timeline.title: Iwami Ginzan
history_timeline.summary: At its peak Iwami Ginzan produced a significant share of the world's silver; Matsudaira Fumai, seventh lord of Matsue, promoted the tea ceremony and wagashi.

history_timeline.title: Lafcadio Hearn
history_timeline.summary: Koizumi Yakumo (Lafcadio Hearn) taught in Matsue and wrote 'Kwaidan'; Iwami Ginzan became World Heritage in 2007.

specialties.name: Lake Shinji clams
specialties.note: One of Lake Shinji's seven delicacies

specialties.name: Matsue wagashi
specialties.note: One of Japan's three great confectionery towns

dialect.name: Izumo dialect
dialect.features: Izumo speech is strikingly similar to Tōhoku dialects ('zūzū-ben'); 'dandan' means thank you.

guide.opening: This old man is a kataribe of Izumo. Every tenth lunar month the eight million gods meet here — so while the rest of Japan calls it 'the month without gods', only Izumo calls it 'the month with gods'. Would you hear this myth?

regional_meme.title: Where is Shimane?
regional_meme.text: Shimane regularly tops surveys of 'the hardest prefecture to find on a map' — locals even made a self-mocking manga, 'The Great Secret of Shimane'.

regional_meme.title: The month with gods
regional_meme.text: Elsewhere the tenth month is 'Kannazuki', the month without gods; only Izumo calls it 'Kamiarizuki' — all of Japan's gods are here for a meeting.

hero_persona.name: Yamanaka Shikanosuke
hero_persona.title: Valiant restorer of the Amago
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Yamanaka Shikanosuke Yukimori! 'Grant me the seven hardships and eight sufferings' — that is what I prayed to the moon to restore the house of Amago.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: loyal, brave and tragic, with an iron will; fiery when recalling the fall of his lord's house

ramen.highlight: Shimane is famous for Izumo soba; ramen here is mostly clear-broth chūka soba

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: unfiltered, undiluted and powerful

meiji_transition.summary: Okayama Prefecture was set up in 1871; in 1876 Oda Prefecture (Bitchū and eastern Bingo) and Hōjō Prefecture (Mimasaka) joined, while part of Bingo went to Hiroshima.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Ancient Kibi was split into Bizen, Bitchū and Bingo; Okayama got the first two and Bingo went to Hiroshima. Mimasaka was carved out of Bizen in 713.

history_timeline.title: The kingdom of Kibi
history_timeline.summary: Ancient Kibi was a regional power that could rival Yamato (witness the Tsukuriyama tumulus); in the 7th century it was split into Bizen, Bitchū and Bingo, and Mimasaka was carved from Bizen in 713.

history_timeline.title: Hōnen and Eisai
history_timeline.summary: Hōnen, founder of Pure Land Buddhism, was born in Mimasaka and Eisai, founder of Rinzai Zen, in Bitchū; the swordsmiths of Osafune in Bizen began to rise.

history_timeline.title: Akamatsu vs. Yamana
history_timeline.summary: The Akamatsu governed Bizen, while Mimasaka and other provinces changed hands between the Akamatsu and Yamana; 'Bizen Osafune' blades became famous throughout the land.

history_timeline.title: Ukita Naoie
history_timeline.summary: Ukita Naoie rose by scheming; his son Hideie became one of Toyotomi's Five Elders and was exiled to Hachijōjima after Sekigahara.

history_timeline.title: Shizutani School
history_timeline.summary: Ikeda Mitsumasa, lord of Okayama, founded the Shizutani School, the oldest surviving school for commoners; Kōrakuen was laid out as a daimyo garden.

history_timeline.title: Land of sunshine
history_timeline.summary: Blessed with many days of almost no rain, Okayama calls itself 'Hare no Kuni'; the Mizushima industrial zone and the Kurashiki historical quarter sit side by side.

landmarks.name: Kōrakuen
landmarks.note: One of Japan's three great gardens

dialect.name: Okayama dialect
dialect.features: Sentences end in '-ja'; 'dēre' (very) is the signature word, and lately 'mongē' has caught on too.

guide.opening: This old man gazes over the Kibi plain from atop the Tsukuriyama tumulus. Legend says the tale of Momotarō fighting the ogres comes from Kibitsuhiko defeating the demon Ura — would you hear it?

regional_meme.title: Who owns Momotarō?
regional_meme.text: Where was Momotarō from? Okayama, Kagawa and Inuyama in Aichi all claim him — and Ogre Island is said to be Megijima in Kagawa.

regional_meme.title: Land of sunshine
regional_meme.text: Okayama prides itself on being 'Hare no Kuni', the sunny land — locals feel cheated when it rains.

hero_persona.name: Ukita Hideie
hero_persona.title: One of Toyotomi's Five Elders · exile of Hachijōjima
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Ukita Hideie, once one of the Toyotomi Five Elders. After Sekigahara I was exiled to Hachijōjima and lived past eighty — I have tasted every rise and fall life has to offer.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: gentle and refined like a young noble, full of longing for Okayama and for Hideyoshi

ramen.highlight: Old-hen meat instead of pork chashu — unique to Kasaoka, a chicken-farming town

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: brewed with the revived Akaiwa Omachi rice, deep and rice-forward

meiji_transition.summary: Hiroshima Prefecture was set up in 1871, and six districts of Bingo were transferred from Okayama in 1876, forming today's borders.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Hiroshima = Aki + Bingo; the Fukuyama area belongs to Bingo, closely tied to Okayama, with a slightly different dialect.

history_timeline.title: Itsukushima Shrine
history_timeline.summary: Legend dates Itsukushima Shrine to 593; Taira no Kiyomori rebuilt it on a grand scale in the 12th century, and its torii in the sea became a symbol.

history_timeline.title: The Aki Takeda and the Mōri
history_timeline.summary: Itsukushima stayed under shogunal protection after the Taira fell; the Takeda governed Aki, and the Mōri's ancestors, a branch of the Ōe, received Yoshida estate in Aki.

history_timeline.title: The Mōri take root
history_timeline.summary: The Mōri made Yoshida-Kōriyama Castle their base and formed a league with neighboring local lords; the Itsukushima area fell under Ōuchi influence.

history_timeline.title: The lesson of the three arrows
history_timeline.summary: Mōri Motonari defeated Sue Harukata at Itsukushima in 1555 and gradually unified the Chūgoku region; legend says he taught his three sons unity with 'three arrows'. Terumoto built Hiroshima Castle in 1589.

history_timeline.title: The Asano of Hiroshima
history_timeline.summary: After Fukushima Masanori was dispossessed, Asano Nagaakira took over Hiroshima; Fukuyama in Bingo went to a fudai lord, and Inland Sea port towns thrived.

history_timeline.title: City of peace
history_timeline.summary: In the Meiji era Hiroshima became a military city (Ujina port, Kure naval district); the atomic bomb fell on 6 August 1945, and the city was rebuilt as a city of peace.

landmarks.name: Itsukushima Shrine
landmarks.note: The great torii in the sea

dialect.name: Hiroshima dialect
dialect.features: '-jaken' (because) is the signature; 'buchi' (very) and 'taigii' (a hassle) are everyday words.

phrases.meaning: what a hassle, can't be bothered

guide.opening: This old man has come to Miyajima just as the tide covers the feet of the great torii. On this very sea Mōri Motonari beat a larger army — would you hear of the Battle of Itsukushima?

regional_meme.title: Don't call it 'Hiroshima-style'
regional_meme.text: In Hiroshima it's just 'okonomiyaki' — add 'Hiroshima-style' and the locals will correct you.

regional_meme.title: The Carp faith
regional_meme.text: Hiroshima's love of the Carp baseball team is near-religious; on game days the whole city turns red.

hero_persona.name: Mōri Motonari
hero_persona.title: The schemer · lesson of the three arrows
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Mōri Motonari. One arrow breaks easily; three together do not — step by step I rose from a petty lord of Aki to master of the Chūgoku region.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: wily yet kindly, loves to talk of family unity and strategy

ramen.broth: Shōyu (chicken and dried sardine, with bits of back fat)
ramen.toppings: Back-fat bits, chashu, scallions, bamboo shoots
ramen.highlight: The savor of Inland Sea dried sardines with dots of back fat — soul food of a town of slopes

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: a venerable brewery of Saijō, home of the soft-water brewing method

meiji_transition.summary: In 1871 Yamaguchi merged with Iwakuni, Tokuyama, Kiyosue, Toyoura and other prefectures to form Yamaguchi Prefecture.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Yamaguchi = Suō + Nagato, almost exactly the Mōri's lands in the Edo period — a textbook case where domain, province and prefecture coincide.

history_timeline.title: Nagato and Dan-no-ura
history_timeline.summary: The Nagato provincial capital was at today's Shimonoseki; in 1185 the Taira were destroyed at Dan-no-ura and the child Emperor Antoku sank into the sea.

history_timeline.title: The Nagato Tandai
history_timeline.summary: After the Mongol invasions the shogunate set up the Nagato Tandai to guard against another attack; the Ōuchi grew strong as provincial officials of Suō.

history_timeline.title: Yamaguchi, Kyoto of the west
history_timeline.summary: Ōuchi Hiroyo made Yamaguchi his base and modeled its streets on Kyoto; Ōuchi Yoshihiro once held six provinces but died in the Ōei Rebellion of 1399.

history_timeline.title: Kyoto of the west
history_timeline.summary: The Ōuchi made Yamaguchi a 'Kyoto of the west' and traded with Ming China and Korea; Francis Xavier preached here. In 1551 Sue Harukata rebelled, and was later destroyed by Mōri Motonari.

history_timeline.title: The Chōshū Domain
history_timeline.summary: After Sekigahara the Mōri were cut back to Suō and Nagato with their seat at Hagi; Yoshida Shōin's Shōka Sonjuku school trained men like Takasugi Shinsaku and Itō Hirobumi.

history_timeline.title: Home of the Restoration
history_timeline.summary: Chōshū allied with Satsuma to overthrow the shogunate; Yamaguchi has produced more prime ministers than any other prefecture.

landmarks.name: Akiyoshidai and Akiyoshidō
landmarks.note: Japan's largest karst plateau and cave

specialties.name: Kawara soba
specialties.note: Green-tea soba served on a hot roof tile

dialect.name: Chōshū dialect
dialect.features: '-choru' (is doing) and '-ccha'; the voices of Bakumatsu activists are often rendered in Chōshū dialect.

phrases.note: said to come from Chōshū speech, later the formal style of the old army

guide.opening: This old man has heard the Heike's laments at Dan-no-ura. Centuries later, the young activists of Chōshū set out from here to topple the shogunate — would you hear of the Shōka Sonjuku?

regional_meme.title: Prefecture of prime ministers
regional_meme.text: Yamaguchi has produced more prime ministers than any other prefecture — a point of local pride.

regional_meme.title: It's 'fuku', not 'fugu'
regional_meme.text: Shimonoseki people call pufferfish 'fuku' (luck) instead of 'fugu', for good fortune.

hero_persona.name: Takasugi Shinsaku
hero_persona.title: Founder of the Kiheitai
hero_persona.opening_line: I'm Takasugi Shinsaku. 'To make this dull world interesting' — that's why I founded the Kiheitai and rose up at Kōzan-ji.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: free-spirited man of action, passionate and poetic; reverent toward his teacher Yoshida Shōin

ramen.highlight: Yamaguchi sits just across the strait from Kyūshū, and tonkotsu culture has taken root in the west of the prefecture

sake.taste_profile: Light & sweet: Yamada Nishiki polished to 23%, with a lush fruity aroma famous worldwide

edo_domains: Tokushima Domain (Hachisuka clan, also ruling Awaji)

meiji_transition.summary: Myōdō Prefecture (including Awaji) was set up in 1871; in 1876 Awa joined Kōchi and Awaji went to Hyōgo, and Tokushima Prefecture was re-established in 1880.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Tokushima = Awa Province; in the Edo period the Tokushima Domain also ruled Awaji, which went to Hyōgo after Meiji, so Awa and Awaji ended up in different prefectures.

history_timeline.title: The Imbe of Awa
history_timeline.summary: Awa's name is said to come from 'awa' (millet); the Imbe clan wove hemp cloth for court rituals here.

history_timeline.title: The Ogasawara enter Awa
history_timeline.summary: After the Jōkyū War the Ogasawara became governors of Awa, and Awa's indigo dyeing began to develop.

history_timeline.title: Hosokawa and Miyoshi
history_timeline.summary: Awa was governed by the Awa branch of the Hosokawa, and their retainers the Miyoshi rose to become masters of the Kinai.

history_timeline.title: The Miyoshi regime
history_timeline.summary: Miyoshi Nagayoshi of Awa once controlled Kyoto and is called 'the first ruler of the realm'; later Chōsokabe Motochika unified Shikoku, and Hideyoshi sent Hachisuka Iemasa to take over.

history_timeline.title: Awa indigo
history_timeline.summary: The Tokushima Domain grew rich on indigo dye and salt; the Awa Odori dance is said to have begun at the celebrations for the completion of Tokushima Castle.

history_timeline.title: Naruto
history_timeline.summary: The Naruto whirlpools and the Ōnaruto Bridge (1985) became its emblems; during WWI German prisoners at the Bandō camp gave Japan's first performance of Beethoven's Ninth.

landmarks.name: Naruto whirlpools
landmarks.note: Among the world's largest tidal whirlpools

landmarks.name: Ryōzen-ji
landmarks.note: Temple No. 1 of the Shikoku pilgrimage

specialties.name: Tokushima ramen
specialties.note: Pork-bone shōyu with a raw egg

dialect.name: Awa dialect
dialect.features: Endings like '-jo' and '-dee'; 'erai' means tired, and 'makemake' means full to overflowing.

guide.opening: I'm a pilgrim of the Shikoku route, just setting out from Temple No. 1, Ryōzen-ji. All eighty-eight temples make a 1,400-km walk — let's talk about Awa's past as we go, shall we?

regional_meme.title: The prefecture without trains
regional_meme.text: Tokushima is the only prefecture in Japan with no electrified railway — every train is a diesel.

regional_meme.title: Awa Odori fever
regional_meme.text: 'The dancers are fools, the watchers are fools — if we're all fools, you might as well dance!' For four days of Obon the whole city goes wild.

hero_persona.name: Miyoshi Nagayoshi
hero_persona.title: The first ruler of the realm
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Miyoshi Nagayoshi, of Awa. Before Nobunaga, I already held Kyoto and the home provinces — yet the world seldom remembers my name.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: calm and cultured, skilled at linked verse; a little wistful at being forgotten by history

ramen.toppings: Sweet-spicy stir-fried pork belly, raw egg, bean sprouts
ramen.highlight: Simmered pork instead of chashu, topped with a raw egg — often eaten with rice

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: a crisp local sake from beside the Naruto Strait

meiji_transition.summary: Kagawa Prefecture was set up in 1871, merged into Myōdō in 1873, restored in 1875, merged into Ehime in 1876, and set up for the third time in 1888.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Kagawa = Sanuki Province, Japan's smallest prefecture; it was merged away and restored three times in the Meiji era before becoming independent for good in 1888.

history_timeline.title: Kūkai's birthplace
history_timeline.summary: Kūkai (Kōbō Daishi) was born near Zentsū-ji in Sanuki; in 821 he led the repair of the Mannō Pond.

history_timeline.title: The vengeful spirit of Sutoku
history_timeline.summary: After the Hōgen Rebellion Retired Emperor Sutoku was exiled to Sanuki and died there, becoming a famous vengeful spirit; in the Kamakura period Sanuki was ruled by shogunal vassals.

history_timeline.title: Domain of the Hosokawa kanrei
history_timeline.summary: Sanuki was ruled directly by the Keichō Hosokawa, the kanrei house, with the 'four guardians of the Hosokawa' — the Kagawa, Kōzai, Yasutomi and others — as deputies.

history_timeline.title: The Chōsokabe invasion
history_timeline.summary: Sanuki's local lords allied with the Miyoshi; in the 1580s Chōsokabe Motochika swallowed Sanuki, which Hideyoshi took back in his Shikoku campaign.

history_timeline.title: The Konpira pilgrimage
history_timeline.summary: Takamatsu (Matsudaira) and Marugame (Kyōgoku) split the province; the 'Konpira pilgrimage' rivaled the Ise pilgrimage as a common dream, and the 'three whites of Sanuki' — salt, sugar and cotton — underpinned the economy.

history_timeline.title: Great Seto Bridge
history_timeline.summary: The Great Seto Bridge opened in 1988, linking Shikoku to Honshū; Kagawa styles itself 'Udon Prefecture' after Sanuki udon.

specialties.name: Honetsuki-dori
specialties.note: Marugame's roast chicken leg on the bone

dialect.name: Sanuki dialect
dialect.features: Endings like '-ken' and '-mai'; 'mandegan' means everything, with an intonation close to Kansai's.

guide.opening: I'm a pilgrim — Master Kūkai was born right here at Zentsū-ji. How about a bowl of udon first, and then I'll tell you how this prefecture was 'founded three times'?

regional_meme.title: Udon Prefecture
regional_meme.text: Kagawa once rebranded itself 'Udon Prefecture'; legend says udon broth flows from the taps here (some facilities really installed them).

regional_meme.title: The gaming ordinance
regional_meme.text: Kagawa passed an ordinance limiting how long children may play video games, sparking a nationwide debate.

hero_persona.name: Kūkai
hero_persona.title: Kōbō Daishi
hero_persona.opening_line: This humble monk is Kūkai, born in Sanuki. I went to Tang China to seek the Dharma and returned to found Shingon Buddhism — my footprints are at all eighty-eight temples of Shikoku.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: profound and compassionate, learned and versatile; speaks of the Dharma, calligraphy and engineering (the Mannō Pond)

ramen.highlight: Ramen keeps a low profile in Udon Prefecture — ask a local and they'll say 'go have udon instead'

sake.taste_profile: Rich & dry: a full-bodied pure-rice sake from the temple town of Konpira

meiji_transition.summary: Sekitetsu and Kamiyama prefectures merged as Ehime in 1873; from 1876 to 1888 it briefly included Sanuki.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Ehime = Iyo Province; the name comes from 'Ehime', the goddess-name of Iyo in the Kojiki (a beautiful maiden).

history_timeline.title: The twin-named island of Iyo
history_timeline.summary: The Kojiki calls Shikoku 'Iyo no Futana-shima', and names Iyo 'Ehime' — the origin of today's prefectural name; Dōgo Onsen appears in the Nihon Shoki.

history_timeline.title: Kōno Michiari and the Mongols
history_timeline.summary: Kōno Michiari of Iyo fought fiercely against the Mongols in 1281 and became famous; Ippen, founder of the Ji sect, was also of the Kōno clan.

history_timeline.title: The Kōno and the Murakami navy
history_timeline.summary: The Kōno held Iyo for generations, while the Murakami navy of the Inland Sea grew powerful, controlling the sea lanes and collecting tolls.

history_timeline.title: The Murakami navy
history_timeline.summary: The missionary Luís Fróis called the Murakami 'the greatest pirates of Japan'; the Kōno ruled central Iyo.

history_timeline.title: The Date of Uwajima
history_timeline.summary: Date Masamune's eldest son Hidemune was given Uwajima; Katō Yoshiaki built Matsuyama Castle, later held by the Matsudaira.

history_timeline.title: Botchan and Shiki
history_timeline.summary: Masaoka Shiki was born in Matsuyama, and Natsume Sōseki set 'Botchan' there; the Shimanami Kaidō (fully opened 2006) links it to Hiroshima.

landmarks.name: Dōgo Onsen Honkan
landmarks.note: One of Japan's oldest hot springs

landmarks.name: Matsuyama Castle
landmarks.note: One of the twelve original keeps

specialties.name: Taimeshi
specialties.note: Uwajima-style raw sea bream over rice

dialect.name: Iyo dialect
dialect.features: A slow, leisurely tone; old Matsuyama's '-zonamoshi' is famous from 'Botchan', and '-ken' is common.

guide.opening: I'm a pilgrim, fresh out of Dōgo Onsen and feeling wonderful. The ships of the Murakami navy once came and went freely on this sea — want to hear some pirate stories?

regional_meme.title: Orange juice from the tap
regional_meme.text: The Ehime legend: turn on the tap and mikan juice comes out — and at Matsuyama Airport it really does.

regional_meme.title: Iyo takes it easy
regional_meme.text: Iyo people speak slowly — 'Iyo nonbiri', the easygoing Iyo — in contrast to the hot-tempered folk of Tosa.

hero_persona.name: Murakami Takeyoshi
hero_persona.title: The greatest pirate in Japan
hero_persona.opening_line: I'm Murakami Takeyoshi, and the Inland Sea is my home! Even the missionaries call me Japan's greatest pirate — any ship passing through pays the toll.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: hearty and bold, a true man of the sea, versed in currents and naval tactics

ramen.highlight: Unlike Nagasaki champon, the broth is clear, Japanese-style and gentle

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: in the sweet-sake tradition of the Inland Sea

meiji_transition.summary: Kōchi Prefecture was set up in 1871 and absorbed Awa from 1876 to 1880.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Kōchi = Tosa Province, squeezed between the Shikoku mountains and the Pacific — long isolated, which gave it a temperament all its own.

history_timeline.title: Land of distant exile
history_timeline.summary: Tosa was a place of distant exile; Ki no Tsurayuki, governor of Tosa, wrote the 'Tosa Diary' (c. 935).

history_timeline.title: The emperor who chose exile
history_timeline.summary: In the Kamakura period Tosa was ruled by eastern vassals; after the Jōkyū War Retired Emperor Tsuchimikado volunteered for exile in Tosa and later moved to Awa.

history_timeline.title: The Hosokawa and the Tosa Ichijō
history_timeline.summary: Tosa's governors were the Hosokawa; during the Ōnin War the former regent Ichijō Norifusa took refuge at Nakamura in Tosa, founding the 'Tosa Ichijō' line.

history_timeline.title: Master of Shikoku
history_timeline.summary: Chōsokabe Motochika unified Shikoku with his part-time farmer-soldiers, the 'ichiryō gusoku', but submitted to Hideyoshi in 1585 and kept only Tosa.

history_timeline.title: Upper and lower samurai
history_timeline.summary: When Yamauchi Kazutoyo took over Tosa, the old Chōsokabe retainers were reduced to 'gōshi' (rural samurai), creating a rigid divide — the background to the rise of the gōshi Sakamoto Ryōma.

history_timeline.title: Freedom and People's Rights
history_timeline.summary: Sakamoto Ryōma brokered the Satsuma–Chōshū Alliance; in early Meiji Itagaki Taisuke launched the Freedom and People's Rights Movement from Kōchi.

specialties.name: Katsuo no tataki
specialties.note: Bonito seared over a straw fire

dialect.name: Tosa dialect
dialect.features: '-zeyo' and '-kini' became famous nationwide through dramas about Ryōma; a stubborn man is an 'igossō' and a spirited woman a 'hachikin'.

guide.opening: I'm a pilgrim — the Tosa stretch is the longest and hardest, called 'the dōjō of ascetic practice'. Sakamoto Ryōma grew up on this very coast gazing at the Pacific — want to hear his story?

regional_meme.title: Bekuhai drinking games
regional_meme.text: Kōchi people are legendary drinkers; at banquets they use 'bekuhai' cups with holes or pointed bottoms, so you can't put them down until they're empty.

regional_meme.title: Ryōma everywhere
regional_meme.text: Ryōma airport, Ryōma sweets, Ryōma statues… Kōchi's love of Ryōma is everywhere.

hero_persona.name: Sakamoto Ryōma
hero_persona.title: Rōnin of Tosa · broker of the Satsuma–Chōshū Alliance
hero_persona.opening_line: I'm Sakamoto Ryōma! Japan needs a good scrubbing — leave it to me to bring Satsuma and Chōshū together!
hero_persona.tone_prompt: bold, optimistic and broad-minded; ends sentences with Tosa dialect like '-zeyo' and '-kini'

ramen.highlight: Served piping hot in an earthenware pot — finish by adding rice to the broth

sake.taste_profile: Light & dry: the model of 'Tosa karakuchi', best with seared bonito

meiji_transition.summary: Fukuoka Prefecture was set up in 1871; Kokura Prefecture (western Buzen) and Mizuma Prefecture (Chikugo) joined in 1876.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Fukuoka = Chikuzen + Chikugo + western Buzen; eastern Buzen (Nakatsu, Usa) went to Ōita, so 'Buzen' was split in two.

history_timeline.title: Dazaifu
history_timeline.summary: Dazaifu governed Kyūshū and handled foreign relations — 'the distant court'; Sugawara no Michizane was exiled here in 901.

history_timeline.title: The Mongol defense wall
history_timeline.summary: Mongol fleets attacked in 1274 and 1281; the shogunate built a stone wall along Hakata Bay and set up the Chinzei Tandai in Hakata.

history_timeline.title: Kyūshū tandai and Hakata merchants
history_timeline.summary: Imagawa Ryōshun, as Kyūshū tandai, subdued the Southern Court's forces; Hakata thrived on trade with Ming China and Korea, fought over by the Ōuchi and Shōni.

history_timeline.title: The struggle for Kyūshū
history_timeline.summary: The Ōtomo, Ryūzōji and Shimazu fought for northern Kyūshū, and Tachibana Muneshige became famous for loyalty and valor; after subduing Kyūshū in 1587, Hideyoshi replanned Hakata ('Taikō machiwari').

history_timeline.title: Kuroda, 520,000 koku
history_timeline.summary: Kuroda Nagamasa was given Chikuzen and built Fukuoka Castle; samurai 'Fukuoka' and merchant 'Hakata' stood side by side as twin towns.

history_timeline.title: Industry and gateway
history_timeline.summary: The government-run Yawata Steel Works opened in 1901, laying the foundation of Japan's heavy industry; Fukuoka became a gateway city facing Asia.

landmarks.name: Dazaifu Tenmangū
landmarks.note: Shrine of Michizane, god of learning

dialect.name: Hakata dialect
dialect.features: '-to?', '-bai' and '-ken'; 'suitō yo' (I like you) is hailed as the cutest confession in Japan.

guide.opening: This humble interpreter of Dutch at Dejima has come to Hakata on official business. Dazaifu here was 'the distant court' that ran all of Kyūshū's foreign affairs — shall I tell you of Sugawara no Michizane?

regional_meme.title: Capital of Kyūshū
regional_meme.text: Fukuoka people assume Fukuoka is the capital of Kyūshū — the other six prefectures: who agreed to that?

regional_meme.title: Hakata vs. Fukuoka
regional_meme.text: The station is 'Hakata' but the city is 'Fukuoka' — the Meiji-era vote on the city's name still rankles with Hakata people.

hero_persona.name: Tachibana Muneshige
hero_persona.title: 'Peerless in the West'
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Tachibana Muneshige. Lord Hideyoshi called me 'peerless in the west'. I lost my lands after Sekigahara and returned to Yanagawa twenty years later — all my life I believed in one word: righteousness.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: composed and resolute, modest and principled; speaks of his father-in-law Tachibana Dōsetsu with deep respect

ramen.toppings: Chashu, wood-ear mushrooms, scallions, pickled ginger, sesame
ramen.highlight: Order your noodle firmness, like 'barikata' — then ask for a 'kaedama' refill

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: an old house in Kyūshū's sweet-sake tradition

edo_domains: Hasunoike, Ogi and Kashima (Saga branch domains)

meiji_transition.summary: Imari Prefecture was set up in 1871 and renamed Saga in 1872; in 1876 it was merged into Mizuma and then into Nagasaki, before being re-established in 1883.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Ancient Hizen was split in two — the east went to Saga, the west to Nagasaki — and Saga was even absorbed into Nagasaki for seven years.

history_timeline.title: Yoshinogari and Hizen
history_timeline.summary: Yoshinogari is among the largest moated settlements of the Yayoi period; the Hizen provincial capital lay at Yamato in today's Saga city.

history_timeline.title: The Matsura bands and the Mongols
history_timeline.summary: The Hizen coast was a front line against the Mongol invasions, and the seafaring warrior bands of Matsura were very active.

history_timeline.title: The Shōni and the Ryūzōji
history_timeline.summary: The Shōni were Hizen's main governors, and their vassals the Ryūzōji rose to power; the seafolk around Matsura were also drawn into wakō piracy.

history_timeline.title: The Bear of Hizen
history_timeline.summary: Ryūzōji Takanobu, 'the Bear of Hizen', died at the Battle of Okitanawate in 1584, and his chief retainer Nabeshima Naoshige inherited real power.

history_timeline.title: The Nabeshima and Arita ware
history_timeline.summary: The potter Yi Sam-pyeong found porcelain stone at Arita, and Arita (Imari) ware was shipped to Europe via Dejima; the Saga Domain built reverberatory furnaces, among the most technically advanced domains of the late Edo period.

history_timeline.title: Satchō Dohi
history_timeline.summary: Saga was one of the four 'Satchō Dohi' domains that led the Restoration — home of Ōkuma Shigenobu and Etō Shinpei; the Saga Rebellion broke out in 1874.

dialect.name: Saga dialect
dialect.features: 'Gabai' (very) became famous through 'Saga no Gabai Bāchan'; endings like '-bai' and '-kusa'.

guide.opening: This humble interpreter came especially to see the kilns of Arita. That Imari plate in your hands may once have been loaded at Dejima and shipped to Holland — shall I tell you the story of porcelain?

regional_meme.title: The Saga song
regional_meme.text: A comedian's song 'Saga-ken' sums up the self-mockery — 'Saga-ken, oh Saga-ken…' — and locals love it as much as it stings.

regional_meme.title: Squeezed between Fukuoka and Nagasaki
regional_meme.text: Wedged between two 'big brothers', Saga is often asked: 'Saga… is that in Nagasaki?'

hero_persona.name: Ōkuma Shigenobu
hero_persona.title: Founder of Waseda · twice prime minister
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Ōkuma Shigenobu! I founded Waseda University — and since a man lives to a hundred and twenty-five, I still have big things ahead of me!
hero_persona.tone_prompt: optimistic and expansive, fond of grand statements; passionate about education and political reform

ramen.highlight: A gentler pork-bone broth than Hakata's, often topped with a raw egg

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: 2011 IWC champion sake — the byword for Saga sake

meiji_transition.summary: Nagasaki Prefecture was set up in 1871 and Iki and Tsushima were added in 1872; the Saga area was absorbed in 1876 and split off again in 1883.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Nagasaki is western Hizen plus the islands of Iki and Tsushima; Tsushima lies only about 50 km from Busan and was long Japan's window on Korea.

history_timeline.title: Frontier guards and beacons
history_timeline.summary: Tsushima and Iki were the front line of defense, with frontier guards (sakimori) and beacon towers; Japan's envoys to Tang China sailed from the Gotō Islands.

history_timeline.title: The tragedy of Tsushima and Iki
history_timeline.summary: In the 1274 Mongol invasion Sō Sukekuni, deputy governor of Tsushima, and Taira no Kagetaka, deputy governor of Iki, were killed, and both islands suffered terribly.

history_timeline.title: The Sō and the wakō
history_timeline.summary: The Sō of Tsushima controlled trade with Korea; in 1419 a Korean army attacked Tsushima (the Ōei Invasion). The seafolk of Matsura were among the main wakō pirates.

history_timeline.title: The Nanban trade
history_timeline.summary: Portuguese ships reached Hirado in 1550, Ōmura Sumitada opened Nagasaki in 1571, and in 1580 Nagasaki was even donated to the Jesuits.

history_timeline.title: Window of the closed country
history_timeline.summary: In 1641 the Dutch trading post moved to Dejima, making Nagasaki Japan's only window on Europe during the closed-country era; after the 1637 Shimabara Rebellion Christianity was banned, and hidden Christians kept their faith for over two centuries.

history_timeline.title: Shipbuilding and the atomic bomb
history_timeline.summary: Mitsubishi's Nagasaki Shipyard drove modern industry; the atomic bomb fell on 9 August 1945; the hidden-Christian heritage sites became World Heritage in 2018.

specialties.name: Nagasaki champon
specialties.note: Seafood noodle soup created by a Chinese immigrant

specialties.name: Shippoku cuisine
specialties.note: A round-table feast blending Japanese, Chinese and Dutch

dialect.name: Nagasaki dialect
dialect.features: '-bai' and 'batten' (but); rich in loanwords from Portuguese, Dutch and Chinese, like 'giyaman' (glass).

guide.opening: Welcome to Dejima! On this little fan-shaped island this humble interpreter translated countless 'fūsetsugaki' reports from the Dutch for the shogunate. All the world's news in the closed-country era came in through here.

regional_meme.title: City of slopes
regional_meme.text: Nagasaki is famous for its hills — plenty of locals never learned to ride a bicycle.

regional_meme.title: The real castella
regional_meme.text: Nagasaki people insist castella from anywhere else isn't the real thing — the coarse sugar on the bottom is its soul.

hero_persona.name: Amakusa Shirō
hero_persona.title: Young leader of the Shimabara Rebellion
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Amakusa Shirō Tokisada. The year I was sixteen, I held Hara Castle together with more than thirty thousand people… would you hear what happened that winter?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: clear, steadfast and compassionate; miracle stories must be marked as legend, and religious incitement avoided

ramen.noodles: Thick noodles made with tōakuku alkaline water
ramen.highlight: Nutritious noodles invented by the Chinese immigrant Chin Heijun for Chinese students

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: an old brewery in Hasami (Nagasaki is better known for Iki barley shōchū)

meiji_transition.summary: Kumamoto and Yatsushiro prefectures were set up in 1871; Kumamoto was renamed Shirakawa in 1872, absorbed Yatsushiro in 1873, and was renamed Kumamoto again in 1876.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Kumamoto = Higo Province; the Sagara of Hitoyoshi in the south ruled the same domain for some 700 years, from Kamakura to Meiji — almost unheard of in Japanese history.

history_timeline.title: Land of fire
history_timeline.summary: Hizen and Higo were anciently called 'Hi no Kuni', the land of fire — the source of legends of Mount Aso and the mysterious 'shiranui' lights; Kikuchi Castle was an ancient Korean-style mountain fort.

history_timeline.title: The Kikuchi and the Mongol scrolls
history_timeline.summary: The Kikuchi were a great power in Kyūshū; the Higo vassal Takezaki Suenaga fought hard against the Mongols and commissioned the 'Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba' scrolls.

history_timeline.title: Prince Kanenaga, Seisei Shōgun
history_timeline.summary: The Kikuchi served the Southern Court's Prince Kanenaga as 'general for subduing the west', seizing Dazaifu in 1361 and briefly controlling Kyūshū, until defeated by Imagawa Ryōshun.

history_timeline.title: The Higo kokujin uprising
history_timeline.summary: Higo was split among many local lords; in 1587 Hideyoshi gave it to Sassa Narimasa, whose rule sparked an uprising and cost him his life. Katō Kiyomasa and Konishi Yukinaga then divided Higo.

history_timeline.title: Kiyomasa and the Hosokawa
history_timeline.summary: Katō Kiyomasa built the 'impregnable' Kumamoto Castle; the Hosokawa (Tadatoshi) took over in 1632, and Miyamoto Musashi wrote 'The Book of Five Rings' here in his last years.

history_timeline.title: The Satsuma Rebellion
history_timeline.summary: In 1877 Saigō's army besieged Kumamoto Castle for over fifty days without success; the 2016 Kumamoto earthquakes badly damaged the castle, and restoration continues.

landmarks.name: Mount Aso
landmarks.note: One of the world's largest calderas

specialties.name: Kumamoto ramen
specialties.note: Pork-bone broth with burnt garlic oil

specialties.name: Karashi renkon
specialties.note: Fried lotus root stuffed with mustard miso

dialect.name: Kumamoto dialect
dialect.features: '-tai' and '-bai'; 'atozeki' (close the door behind you) is unique to Kumamoto, and a 'mokkosu' is a stubborn Kumamoto man.

guide.opening: This humble interpreter stands beneath the 'mushagaeshi' walls of Kumamoto Castle — curved stone that kept Saigō's army out for over fifty days. Shall I tell you how Katō Kiyomasa built it?

regional_meme.title: Director Kumamon
regional_meme.text: Kumamon is officially Kumamoto Prefecture's 'Sales Director and Director of Happiness' — busier than most human civil servants.

regional_meme.title: Higo mokkosu
regional_meme.text: Kumamoto men are famous for stubbornness: once they decide something, not even nine oxen can pull them back.

hero_persona.name: Katō Kiyomasa
hero_persona.title: Master castle builder · 'Toranosuke'
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Katō Kazuenokami Kiyomasa! I hunted a tiger, they say, and I built a castle in Kumamoto — Saigō's men spent fifty days at these 'mushagaeshi' walls and never got over!
hero_persona.tone_prompt: fierce and hearty, straightforward; bursting with pride about Kumamoto Castle; the tiger hunt is legend

ramen.toppings: Burnt garlic oil (mā-yu), fried garlic chips, wood-ear mushrooms, nori
ramen.highlight: The black burnt-garlic oil is its soul — intensely fragrant

sake.taste_profile: Rich & sweet: birthplace of 'Kumamoto yeast' (Yeast No. 9)

meiji_transition.summary: Ōita Prefecture was set up in 1871, and in 1876 the Shimoge and Usa districts of Kokura Prefecture were added.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: In the Edo period Bungo was split into eight small domains plus shogunal land — 'a land of small domains' — so dialect and customs still vary a lot across the prefecture.

history_timeline.title: Usa Jingū
history_timeline.summary: Usa Jingū is the head shrine of all Hachiman shrines in Japan; the Kunisaki Peninsula developed the 'Rokugō Manzan' fusion of Shintō and Buddhism.

history_timeline.title: The Ōtomo arrive
history_timeline.summary: The Kantō vassal Ōtomo Yoshinao was made governor of Bungo, and the Ōtomo ruled Bungo for some four hundred years.

history_timeline.title: The Ōtomo expand
history_timeline.summary: The Ōtomo also governed Buzen and Chikugo and fought the Ōuchi and Shōni for northern Kyūshū; Usa Jingū flourished under their protection.

history_timeline.title: Ōtomo Sōrin
history_timeline.summary: The Christian daimyo Ōtomo Sōrin controlled six provinces of northern Kyūshū at his peak and helped send the Tenshō boy envoys to Europe; after losing to the Shimazu at Mimikawa in 1578, the Ōtomo declined.

history_timeline.title: A land of small domains
