history_timeline.summary: After the Ōtomo were dispossessed, Bungo was divided among many small domains; Fukuzawa Yukichi of Nakatsu and the thinker Miura Baien came from here.

history_timeline.title: Hot Spring Prefecture
history_timeline.summary: Beppu and Yufuin give Ōita Japan's largest number of hot-spring sources and greatest flow; it is also known for the 'One Village, One Product' movement.

landmarks.name: Yufuin
landmarks.note: Hot spring town beneath Mount Yufu

specialties.name: Seki saba and Seki aji
specialties.note: Line-caught mackerel and horse mackerel of the Hōyo Strait

dialect.name: Ōita dialect
dialect.features: 'Yodakii' (can't be bothered) and 'shinken' (very) are signature words, with endings like '-cha' and '-ccha'.

phrases.meaning: too much trouble, can't be bothered

guide.opening: While soaking in a Beppu hot spring, this humble interpreter heard that Ōtomo Sōrin once sent four boys all the way to Rome to meet the Pope — shall I tell you of the Tenshō embassy?

regional_meme.title: The 'Onsen Prefecture' trademark war
regional_meme.text: Ōita branded itself 'Onsen-ken' (Hot Spring Prefecture) — and Gunma and other hot-spring giants protested at once: who said you could have it?

regional_meme.title: Beppu's steam
regional_meme.text: Hot-spring steam rises all over Beppu's streets; first-time visitors often think something's on fire.

hero_persona.name: Ōtomo Sōrin
hero_persona.title: Christian daimyo
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Ōtomo Sōrin, lord of Bungo. I once held six provinces of northern Kyūshū and sent young envoys all the way to Rome — would you hear of the wonders of the Nanban lands?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: refined and lavish, insatiably curious; passionate about Nanban culture and the tea ceremony

ramen.highlight: Hearty ramen for fishing-port workers, with a generous hand on the garlic

sake.taste_profile: Shōchū: Ōita's signature barley shōchū, nicknamed 'the Napoleon of the shitamachi'

meiji_transition.summary: Mimitsu and Miyakonojō prefectures merged into Miyazaki in 1873, which was absorbed into Kagoshima in 1876 and re-established in 1883.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Southwest Morokata District of Hyūga belonged to the Satsuma Domain, and after Meiji part of it (Shibushi and others) went to Kagoshima — so Miyazaki is a little smaller than ancient Hyūga.

history_timeline.title: Descent of the heavenly grandson
history_timeline.summary: Takachiho is the setting of the myth of the heavenly grandson's descent, and Emperor Jinmu's legendary eastern expedition set out from Hyūga; the Saitobaru tomb group is vast.

history_timeline.title: The Itō receive Hyūga
history_timeline.summary: Descendants of Kudō Suketsune, the Itō, were granted stewardships in Hyūga and moved there for good in the Northern and Southern Courts era.

history_timeline.title: Itō and Shimazu
history_timeline.summary: The Itō expanded across Hyūga and fought the Shimazu to the south for it, beginning a long rivalry.

history_timeline.title: Itō vs. Shimazu
history_timeline.summary: Itō Yoshisuke once held the 'forty-eight castles of Itō', but lost to Shimazu Yoshihiro at Kizakibaru in 1572 and fled to the Ōtomo, triggering the 1578 Battle of Mimikawa.

history_timeline.title: A forest of small domains
history_timeline.summary: Nobeoka, Takanabe, Obi and Sadowara stood side by side; Obi cedar and the Obi castle town survive today.

history_timeline.title: Sunny Miyazaki
history_timeline.summary: Re-established in 1883; in the 1960s–70s it was Japan's honeymoon destination, and today it is known for mangoes and pro-baseball spring camps.

dialect.name: Miyazaki dialect
dialect.features: 'Tege' (very) and 'yodakii', with a slow tone; around Morokata the speech is close to Satsuma's.

guide.opening: This humble interpreter has come to Takachiho Gorge, where legend says Amaterasu hid in the Heavenly Rock Cave — shall I begin in the age of the gods?

regional_meme.title: 'Nothing but nature'
regional_meme.text: Miyazaki is often told it has 'nothing but nature'; a former governor's line 'We've got to do something about Miyazaki' became a catchphrase.

regional_meme.title: Tegetege
regional_meme.text: 'Tegetege' — good enough is good enough: Miyazaki's laid-back philosophy.

hero_persona.name: Komura Jutarō
hero_persona.title: Diplomat from Obi
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Komura Jutarō, born in the Obi Domain. The Portsmouth peace talks, the revision of the unequal treaties — I spent my whole life at the negotiating table.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: calm, practical and well-ordered, with a diplomat's sense of proportion

ramen.highlight: Pickled daikon is often set out on the table as a side

sake.taste_profile: Shōchū: sweet-potato shōchū made with black kōji, often Japan's best-seller

meiji_transition.summary: Kagoshima Prefecture was set up in 1871 and absorbed Miyazaki in 1876 (split off in 1883); the Amami Islands also belong to Kagoshima.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Kagoshima = Satsuma + Ōsumi + part of Hyūga, plus the Amami Islands — once part of the Ryukyu Kingdom, taken under Satsuma's direct control after 1609.

history_timeline.title: The Hayato
history_timeline.summary: The Hayato of southern Kyūshū resisted the court (the Hayato Rebellion of 720) before being brought into the ritsuryō system; Ōsumi was split from Hyūga in 713.

history_timeline.title: The Shimazu arrive
history_timeline.summary: Koremune no Tadahisa was made steward of the Shimazu estate and governor of Satsuma, Ōsumi and Hyūga, taking the name Shimazu and beginning some seven centuries of rule.

history_timeline.title: The Shimazu unite Satsuma and Ōsumi
history_timeline.summary: In the Northern and Southern Courts era the Shimazu split into the Sōshū and Ōshū branches; in the Muromachi period they gradually unified Satsuma and Ōsumi, while the Tanegashima clan held Tanegashima.

history_timeline.title: The four Shimazu brothers
history_timeline.summary: Yoshihisa, Yoshihiro, Toshihisa and Iehisa nearly unified Kyūshū before submitting to Hideyoshi in 1587; at Sekigahara Yoshihiro broke straight through the Eastern lines in the 'Shimazu retreat'.

history_timeline.title: The Satsuma Domain
history_timeline.summary: Satsuma trained its samurai through the 'gōjū' youth system and controlled the Ryukyu Kingdom to profit from trade with China; Zusho Hirosato carried out its financial reforms.

history_timeline.title: The Meiji Restoration
history_timeline.summary: Saigō Takamori and Ōkubo Toshimichi drove the Restoration; in the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion Saigō died at Shiroyama. (Tanegashima, where firearms reached Japan in 1543, is also in the prefecture.)

landmarks.name: Yakushima
landmarks.note: World Natural Heritage, home of the Jōmon cedar

dialect.name: Satsuma dialect
dialect.features: Famously hard to understand — said to have served as a code in the Bakumatsu era; 'Chesto!' is a battle cry, and 'oyattosaa' means good work.

phrases.meaning: good work, thanks for your effort

guide.opening: This humble interpreter is watching the smoke from Sakurajima — Satsuma folk live with volcanic ash every day. At Sekigahara, Shimazu Yoshihiro cut his way out straight through the enemy lines — shall I tell you?

regional_meme.title: Ashfall forecasts
regional_meme.text: Kagoshima's weather report includes an 'ashfall forecast' for Sakurajima — check the wind before you hang out the laundry.

regional_meme.title: Satsuma hayato
regional_meme.text: Kagoshima men are known for their uprightness — 'gironwa muyō' (no lectures, please) is the Satsuma spirit.

hero_persona.name: Saigō Takamori
hero_persona.title: One of the three heroes of the Restoration
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Saigō Kichinosuke. 'Revere Heaven, love people' — for this country, I would give up both my life and my name.
hero_persona.tone_prompt: generous, plain-spoken and loyal, with a Satsuma accent ('oidon', '-degowasu')

ramen.toppings: Chashu, scallions, fried onion, bean sprouts
ramen.highlight: Lighter than Hakata's — and pickled daikon and tea arrive as soon as you sit down

sake.taste_profile: Shōchū: one of the 'three Ms', a dream sweet-potato shōchū brewed in earthenware jars

sengoku_daimyo: Second Shō dynasty (King Shō Shin, King Shō Nei)
edo_domains: Ryukyu Kingdom (under Satsuma control after 1609, while paying tribute to Ming and Qing China)

meiji_transition.summary: The Ryukyu Domain was created in 1872, and in 1879 the 'Ryukyu Disposition' abolished it and created Okinawa Prefecture; from 1945 to 1972 Okinawa was under US rule, returning to Japan in 1972.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Ryukyu never had ritsuryō provinces; the Amami Islands were part of the Ryukyu Kingdom until Satsuma took them after 1609, and they still belong to Kagoshima.

history_timeline.title: The Three Kingdoms and old Ryukyu
history_timeline.summary: The Ryukyu Islands lay outside the ritsuryō state; from the 12th century local lords (aji) built stone castles (gusuku), and three kingdoms — Hokuzan, Chūzan and Nanzan — gradually formed.

history_timeline.title: Aji and gusuku
history_timeline.summary: Lords across the islands built stone gusuku castles and vied for power; legend says the Eiso dynasty arose at Urasoe.

history_timeline.title: Three kingdoms and tribute
history_timeline.summary: Hokuzan, Chūzan and Nanzan stood side by side and began paying tribute to Ming China from 1372, drawing Ryukyu into East Asian maritime trade.

history_timeline.title: The Ryukyu Kingdom
history_timeline.summary: Shō Hashi unified the three kingdoms in 1429; under King Shō Shin power was centralized, and Ryukyu thrived in East Asian sea trade as a 'bridge between nations'.

history_timeline.title: Dual subordination
history_timeline.summary: In 1609 Satsuma invaded Shuri; from then on Ryukyu paid tribute to China while under Satsuma's control — a unique 'dual subordination'.

history_timeline.title: Okinawa Prefecture
history_timeline.summary: The prefecture was created by the Ryukyu Disposition of 1879; the 1945 Battle of Okinawa took a terrible toll on civilians, and US rule lasted until the 1972 reversion.

landmarks.name: Shuri Castle
landmarks.note: Royal castle of the Ryukyu Kingdom

specialties.name: Okinawa soba
specialties.note: Wheat noodles with braised pork belly

dialect.name: Okinawan (Uchināguchi)
dialect.features: The Ryukyuan languages share roots with Japanese but are barely mutually intelligible, with mainly three vowels (a, i, u); 'nankurunaisa' sums up the islanders' optimism.

phrases.phrase: はいさい / はいたい

guide.opening: Haisai~ I'm a noro priestess who guards the sacred utaki. Ryukyu was never one of the ritsuryō provinces — we had our own king and our own sea. Shall I tell you about Shuri Castle, or the seafaring age of the 'bridge between nations'?

regional_meme.title: Okinawa time
regional_meme.text: 'Uchinā taimu' — meeting times in Okinawa tend to run a little late, and nobody minds much.

regional_meme.title: It gets cold in winter too
regional_meme.text: When it drops to 15 °C, Okinawans pull out their down jackets — while mainland tourists stroll by in T-shirts.

hero_persona.name: Shō Hashi
hero_persona.title: King who unified the Three Kingdoms of Ryukyu
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Shō Hashi. Hokuzan, Chūzan and Nanzan split the land for a century — I joined them into one, and from then on Ryukyu faced the sea of all nations!
hero_persona.tone_prompt: broad-minded, bold and far-sighted; often speaks of sea trade and the 'bridge between nations'

ramen.toppings: Braised pork belly or soft-bone ribs, fish cake, pickled ginger
ramen.highlight: No buckwheat, yet specially allowed to be called 'soba' — 17 October is 'Okinawa Soba Day'

sake.taste_profile: Awamori: Okinawa's 'island spirit', made from Thai rice with black kōji

spots.scene: In late-Meiji Hokkaido, Abashiri Prison holds a key to the hunt for the hidden gold; the museum's radial cell blocks are the very ones the story draws on.
spots.tips: The grounds are large with a lot of outdoor walking — dress warmly and watch for ice in winter. It is a historical site, so keep your voice down.

spots.scene: The story's Ezo Agricultural High School is modeled on the author's alma mater, Obihiro Agricultural High, with its vast pastures and school buildings.
spots.tips: This is a working school: it is not open to casual visitors. View it from the public road, stay out of the pastures and do not photograph students.

spots.work: The Age of Lions (Shishi no Jidai)
spots.scene: The drama depicts the Battle of Hakodate and the short-lived Republic of Ezo; Goryōkaku was the last stronghold of the former shogunate forces.
spots.tips: Climb the neighboring Goryōkaku Tower to see the star-shaped fort as a whole. It gets crowded in cherry-blossom season — go early.

spots.scene: Makoto, a witch in training, moves in with relatives in Hirosaki; the castle town, Mount Iwaki and the apple orchards run through the whole series.
spots.tips: Hirosaki Park's spring blossoms and the town's Western-style buildings make a lovely walk. The homes in the series are ordinary houses — please don't disturb residents.

spots.scene: After defeat in the Boshin War, the Aizu clan was moved to the Tonami Domain on the Shimokita Peninsula; the drama shows its retainers struggling in this cold land.
spots.tips: Mutsu City has memorials and displays on the Tonami Domain. Public transport on the peninsula is sparse — drive or check bus times in advance.

spots.work: The House of the Lost on the Cape
spots.scene: After the 2011 earthquake, girls start a new life in the "Mayoiga" house of a seaside town modeled on Ōtsuchi, which collaborated with the film.
spots.tips: This area was rebuilt after the disaster; visit with respect. The coastal reconstruction memorials tell the town's story.

spots.scene: A drama of the rise and fall of the Ōshū Fujiwara; the Heian-period buildings built for filming became a theme park that still serves many period dramas.
spots.tips: The park recreates Hiraizumi-style palaces — great for period-style photos. Pair it with Chūson-ji and Mōtsū-ji in Hiraizumi.

spots.scene: Seven idols based in Sendai start from nothing; the station plaza and city streets appear again and again.
spots.tips: The pedestrian decks and shopping arcades around Sendai Station are familiar scenes. Don't block foot traffic when taking photos.

spots.scene: One of the highest-rated taiga dramas ever, telling the life of Date Masamune; Zuihōden is his mausoleum.
spots.tips: The mausoleum sits at the top of stone steps in a cedar grove, with ornate Momoyama-style decoration. It is a grave site — please be quiet.

spots.scene: The author, Yaguchi Takao, was born in Masuda, Yokote; the clear streams and mountain villages of the series come from his hometown. The museum holds a large collection of his original art.
spots.tips: Masuda is a traditional district of "uchigura" storehouse homes, worth a stroll. Follow the no-photo signs in the original-art galleries.

spots.scene: Part two of the drama covers the Later Three Years' War, whose final battle was fought at the Kanezawa stockade in Dewa — the foundation of the Ōshū Fujiwara.
spots.tips: The battlefield is now Kanezawa Park and Kanezawa Hachimangū; the nearby museum of the Later Three Years' War explains the battle. Lovely in autumn colors.

spots.scene: A Studio Ghibli film: Taeko, a Tokyo office worker, helps with the safflower harvest in rural Yamagata and remembers herself as a fifth-grader.
spots.tips: The Takase area of Yamagata City is the model for the safflower fields, which bloom around July. The fields are private farmland — admire them from the road.

spots.scene: Naoe Kanetsugu serves Uesugi Kagekatsu; after Sekigahara the Uesugi were reduced to Yonezawa, where Kanetsugu spent the rest of his life.
spots.tips: Uesugi Shrine and the Keishōden treasure house on the castle grounds hold the clan's heirlooms. Don't miss Yonezawa beef.

spots.scene: A story centered on the Shinsengumi, which in its later part follows them to Aizu; Mount Iimori is where the young Byakkotai met their tragic end in the Boshin War.
spots.tips: The hill has the Byakkotai graves and the unusual Sazaedō hall — please be respectful. The stone steps are steep; a paid escalator is available.

spots.scene: Aizu-born Niijima Yae took up a rifle to defend Tsuruga Castle; the drama's siege of Aizu happened here.
spots.tips: The keep houses a local museum with views over the Aizu basin from the top. The red-tiled keep looks best with spring blossoms.

spots.scene: The heroines' Ōarai Girls' Academy calls Ōarai its home port; the shopping streets and the torii on the rocks by the sea appear throughout — a model of anime–town collaboration.
spots.tips: The shopping streets are full of character standees and tie-in goods; supporting local shops is part of the pilgrimage. The torii stands on rocks — keep away at high tide or in big waves.

spots.scene: The last shogun came from the Mito Tokugawa and was educated at the domain school Kōdōkan, where he also confined himself after returning power to the emperor.
spots.tips: Kōdōkan is right by Mito Station; in plum season, combine it with Kairakuen garden.

spots.scene: In the first episode, "Cherry Blossom", the station where Takaki waits through the heavy snow is Iwafune on the JR Ryōmō Line.
spots.tips: It is a working station: don't linger on the platform for photos or get in passengers' way. A snowy winter day is closest to the film's mood.

spots.scene: Girls in Nikko form an ice hockey team; the series works with the local pro team, the H.C. Tochigi Nikko Ice Bucks, whose home rink is this arena.
spots.tips: Catching a live game in season gives the best atmosphere; Tōshō-gū and Kegon Falls fit into the same day.

spots.scene: The hero, Ashikaga Takauji, came from the Ashikaga of Ashikaga Estate in Shimotsuke; Bannaji stands on the site of their residence.
spots.tips: The temple keeps its moat and earthen walls, the layout of a warrior's residence. The neighboring Ashikaga School is said to be Japan's oldest school.

spots.scene: Mount Akina, where Takumi delivers tofu, is modeled on Mount Haruna; its run of hairpin bends is the series' most iconic setting.
spots.tips: These are public roads — never imitate the racing. Lake Haruna and Ikaho Onsen are best enjoyed slowly.

spots.work: A Place Further than the Universe
spots.scene: Four girls set out for Antarctica; the hometown and daily life of the lead, Tamaki Mari, are drawn from Tatebayashi.
spots.tips: The station and the streets and riverbanks of Tatebayashi appear in the series. Tatebayashi is famously hot in summer — guard against heatstroke.

spots.scene: Numata Castle, contested by the Sanada and the Hōjō, is a key setting; the dispute became Hideyoshi's pretext for attacking the Hōjō.
spots.tips: The castle site is now Numata Park, overlooking river terraces; the nearby Nagurumi Castle site belongs to the same story.

spots.work: Anohana: The Flower We Saw That Day
spots.scene: A coming-of-age story set in Chichibu; the old bridge appears in the opening and many scenes, and the city has worked with the series for years.
spots.tips: The shopping streets near Chichibu Station and Jōrin-ji temple are also locations. The old bridge is pedestrian-only — mind other walkers.

spots.scene: The Hiiragi sisters' family shrine is modeled on Washinomiya Shrine, often seen as one of the starting points of Japan's anime pilgrimage boom.
spots.tips: It is a real shrine with normal shrine etiquette. The anime-illustrated ema plaques are a highlight, but please don't read out or photograph other people's wishes.

spots.work: Reach Beyond the Blue Sky (Seiten o Tsuke)
spots.scene: The life of Shibusawa Eiichi, "father of Japanese capitalism", born in Chiaraijima village in Musashi — today's Fukaya.
spots.tips: His family home, Naka-no-ie, is nearby. Fukaya leeks are the local specialty, best in winter.

spots.scene: Hikigaya Hachiman is a high-schooler who proudly calls himself a Chiba fan; Chiba City's seafront and streets appear again and again.
spots.tips: The artificial beach at Inage Seaside Park is a fine place for sunset. The series' school is modeled on a real high school — please don't enter the grounds.

spots.place: Awa (Minamoto no Yoritomo landing site, Kyonan)
spots.scene: Defeated at Ishibashiyama, Minamoto no Yoritomo fled across the sea to Awa, regrouped here and went on to found the Kamakura shogunate.
spots.tips: A monument marks Yoritomo's landing on the Kyonan coast; Nihon-ji temple on nearby Mount Nokogiri overlooks Tokyo Bay.

spots.scene: Socially anxious guitarist Hitori Gotoh joins Kessoku Band in Shimokitazawa, a neighborhood packed with live houses.
spots.tips: Shimokitazawa is all vintage shops, small theaters and live houses — catching a live show is the most fitting pilgrimage. The lanes are narrow; don't block them for photos.

spots.scene: The film's iconic staircase with red railings is the Otoko-zaka steps in front of Suga Shrine.
spots.tips: This is a quiet residential area: don't linger in the middle of the stairs or make noise. Weekday mornings are quietest.

spots.place: Edo Castle site (East Gardens of the Imperial Palace)
spots.scene: Atsuhime of Satsuma marries into the shogun's family, lives through the end of the shogunate in the Ōoku, and helps bring about the bloodless surrender of Edo Castle.
spots.tips: The East Gardens are free to enter (closed some days), with the keep foundation and Honmaru site; bags are checked at the gate.

spots.scene: The crossing in the anime opening, with the Enoden train passing in front of the sea, has become a must-see for fans from around the world.
spots.tips: It is extremely crowded. Locals repeatedly ask visitors not to stand in the road for photos, not to block trains or cars, and not to make noise near homes.

spots.scene: The spiritual center of the Kamakura shogunate; Minamoto no Sanetomo's assassination on its great stone steps is one of the drama's most shocking turns.
spots.tips: Walk from Kamakura Station along the Dankazura approach. New Year and weekends are packed — weekday mornings are best.

spots.scene: High-school girls build things by hand in a DIY club, set in Sanjō, a city famous for blades and metalwork that collaborates with the series.
spots.tips: Sanjō is a city of craftspeople — try forging a small knife at a local smithing workshop. Factories are working sites; don't enter without permission.

spots.scene: Naoe Kanetsugu grew up at Kasugayama, the castle of Uesugi Kenshin, and much of the drama's first half takes place here.
spots.tips: It is a hilltop castle site — wear good walking shoes. The main enclosure at the top looks out over the Takada plain and the Sea of Japan.

spots.scene: Nanto is home to the studio P.A.WORKS; Jōhana's old streets, station and Hikiyama festival all appear in the series.
spots.tips: Jōhana is a quiet town of old streets, best explored on foot. Trains on the Jōhana Line are infrequent — check times in advance.

spots.scene: At Kurikara Pass, Kiso Yoshinaka routed the Taira army with his "fire oxen" stratagem; the drama portrays this battle that turned the Genpei War.
spots.tips: The battlefield is in the hills with sloping paths, loveliest when the double cherries bloom in spring. The road is narrow — drive carefully.

spots.scene: Ohana grows up working at the inn Kissuisō; the spa town is modeled on Yuwaku Onsen outside Kanazawa, which even started holding the series' Bonbori Festival for real.
spots.tips: Yuwaku is a quiet mountain spa — don't wander into inns' private areas for photos. It gets crowded during the autumn Bonbori Festival.

spots.scene: Maeda Toshiie took Kanazawa and laid the foundations of the "one-million-koku" Kaga domain; Kanazawa Castle was home to fourteen generations of the Maeda.
spots.tips: The castle sits next to Kenroku-en, so visit both together. Its many styles of stone wall earn it the name "museum of stone walls".

spots.scene: A summer between a girl raised in a glass workshop and a transfer student, set in the seaside town of Mikuni in Sakai, Fukui.
spots.tips: Mikuni's old streets and shore are good for walking. The nearby Tōjinbō cliffs have no railings — keep well back from the edge.

spots.scene: After leaving Mino, Akechi Mitsuhide drifted to Echizen and served Asakura Yoshikage; the drama's Echizen years center on Ichijōdani.
spots.tips: A Sengoku-period street has been reconstructed, giving a feel for a castle town. The site is large — allow half a day.

spots.scene: Koguma, a high-schooler living alone, buys a used Honda Super Cub, and her days unfold on the mountain roads of Hokuto.
spots.tips: Follow traffic rules on bikes or in cars — the mountain roads are winding. The school is modeled on a real high school; don't enter the grounds.

spots.scene: The lakeside where Rin camps alone and meets Nadeshiko in the first episode is Lake Motosu, with its view of Mount Fuji.
spots.tips: Camp only at proper campsites and take all your rubbish home. Winter by the lake is bitterly cold; never light fires where they're banned.

spots.scene: The story of Yamamoto Kansuke, strategist to Takeda Shingen; the Takeda residence at Tsutsujigasaki stood where Takeda Shrine is today.
spots.tips: The original moat and earthworks survive around the shrine; buses run directly from Kōfu Station.

spots.work: Waiting in the Summer (Ano Natsu de Matteru)
spots.scene: Over a summer of making a home-made movie, Komoro's station, Kaikoen park and streets become the story's stage.
spots.tips: Kaikoen, the Komoro Castle site beside the station, is worth a visit; the series displays are in the station and tourist facilities.

spots.scene: The hero follows a senior to her family home in Ueda, Shinshū — the Jinnouchi clan, descendants of the Sanada — where a battle across the internet begins.
spots.tips: Ueda Station and the city have displays about the film. The great house is fictional and the hillsides it draws on are private land — please stay out.

spots.scene: Ueda Castle, built by Sanada Masayuki, twice repelled great Tokugawa armies — the pride of the Sanada.
spots.tips: The Sanada Stone and the West Turret are highlights; spring blossoms and autumn leaves are the best seasons.

spots.scene: The Classics Club's everyday mysteries take place in Kamiyama, modeled on Hida-Takayama, with its old streets, shrines and festivals.
spots.tips: Takayama's old streets are crowded — keep the narrow lanes clear when taking photos. The school is modeled on a real high school; don't enter the grounds.

spots.scene: Searching for Mitsuha, Taki comes to Hida and asks around at Hida-Furukawa's station and streets.
spots.tips: The view of trains from the station footbridge is the classic shot — don't block passengers. The Seto River and white-walled storehouses are lovely for a stroll.

spots.scene: Two generations of "stealing a province": Saitō Dōsan ruled from Inabayama Castle, which Oda Nobunaga took and renamed Gifu.
spots.tips: Ride the Mount Kinka ropeway up; the keep looks out over the Nōbi plain. Cormorant fishing on the Nagara River is famous in summer.

spots.scene: The nine members of Aqours live in Uchiura, Numazu; Awashima island in the bay and the coastal villages are full of traces of the series.
spots.tips: Uchiura is a residential fishing village — keep your voice down and don't linger outside homes. Numazu has many tie-in shops; supporting them is part of the pilgrimage.

spots.scene: The author Momoko Sakura's hometown, Shimizu in Shizuoka City, is Maruko's town; a harbor-side mall has a theme attraction for the series.
spots.tips: The attraction is by Shimizu port, where you can also see Mount Fuji across the harbor. Shimizu is known for its tuna dishes.

spots.scene: Ryōtan-ji in Iinoya is the family temple of the Ii, and the story of the woman lord Ii Naotora protecting her clan centers on this area.
spots.tips: The temple garden is celebrated — please be quiet inside. Iinoya-gū shrine and related memorials are nearby.

spots.scene: Everyday life with Nagoya-loving high-schooler Yatogame and a transfer student, packed with jokes about Nagoya dialect and food.
spots.tips: Nagoya Castle's restored Honmaru Palace is exquisite; afterwards try the "Nagoya-meshi" from the series — miso katsu, tebasaki and more.

spots.work: What Will You Do, Ieyasu? (Dōsuru Ieyasu)
spots.scene: Tokugawa Ieyasu was born at Okazaki Castle in Mikawa, where the drama begins his life of "what will you do?"
spots.tips: Okazaki Park around the castle has an Ieyasu museum, and the old Hatchō miso makers nearby offer tours.

spots.work: Half a Moon Rises in the Sky (Hanbun no Tsuki ga Noboru Sora)
spots.scene: A hospitalized boy and a seriously ill girl, in the author's hometown of Ise.
spots.tips: Combine it with a visit to Ise Jingū. The hospital is modeled on a real one — please don't go in to take photos.

spots.work: Nagi-Asu: A Lull in the Sea
spots.scene: A story of children from an undersea village and a seaside town; the harbor town on land is modeled on the Kumano area of Mie.
spots.tips: Kumano's coastline is spectacular — see Shichiri-mihama beach and Shishi-iwa rock. Fishing ports are workplaces; don't get in the way.

spots.work: What Will You Do, Ieyasu? (Dōsuru Ieyasu)
spots.scene: After the Honnō-ji Incident, Ieyasu fled from Sakai back to Mikawa over the Iga mountains — the drama's tense "crossing of Iga" passes through this land of ninja.
spots.tips: Iga-Ueno Castle's tall stone walls are striking, and the Iga-ryū Ninja Museum below has live ninja demonstrations.

spots.scene: Sakuragaoka High, where the five members of the light music club study, is modeled on the old Toyosato Elementary School in Shiga — especially its staircase with the tortoise-and-hare statues.
spots.tips: The old buildings are open to the public with a fan space; they are a town facility, so keep to the opening hours and house rules.

spots.work: Gō: Princesses of the Warring States
spots.scene: The three daughters of Azai Nagamasa and Oichi — Chacha, Hatsu and Gō — were born at Odani Castle, where the drama begins and where they first saw a castle fall.
spots.tips: Odani is a steep mountain castle; the climb takes one to two hours, so wear proper shoes. The museum at the foot explains the Azai family first.

spots.scene: The Kitauji High concert band story is set in Uji; the riverside, Uji Bridge and the Mount Daikichi lookout are famous scenes.
spots.tips: The Uji riverside is a pleasant walk; the Daikichi lookout needs a short climb. The school is modeled on a real high school — don't enter the grounds.

spots.scene: Tamako, daughter of a mochi shop, and everyday life on a shopping street modeled on Kyoto's Demachi Masugata arcade.
spots.tips: It's where locals do their shopping — don't block shop fronts for photos. Buying something is the best kind of pilgrimage.

spots.scene: When Kondō Isami and his men came to Kyoto they were quartered in Mibu — first known as the "Mibu rōnin" — and trained and gathered at Mibu-dera.
spots.tips: The temple has the graves of Shinsengumi members (Mibuzuka); the nearby former Yagi residence, their headquarters, is open to visitors.

spots.scene: Set in an old shopping arcade in Abeno, Osaka, where two kids defend their streets through one alternate world after another.
spots.tips: Today's Abeno is full of high-rises — go up Abeno Harukas for a view over Osaka. Tennōji Zoo and Tsūtenkaku are nearby.

spots.scene: The title "Sanada Maru" is the outwork Sanada Nobushige built on the south side of Osaka Castle in the Winter Siege; the drama climaxes in the Siege of Osaka.
spots.tips: Osaka Castle Park is huge and the keep is a museum; Sankō Shrine south of the castle has sites linked to the Sanada Maru.

spots.scene: Girls who dream of becoming stars of a revue company modeled on the Takarazuka Revue; the town and its "Hana no Michi" promenade appear.
spots.tips: Hana no Michi is a nice walk. Near the theater, please don't follow or photograph performers and students.

spots.scene: Kuroda Kanbei came from Harima and offered Himeji Castle to Hashiba Hideyoshi as his base for conquering western Japan.
spots.tips: Expect queues to climb the keep of this World Heritage castle — go early in high season. Stairs inside are steep and shoes come off.

spots.scene: A girl spirit warrior and a half-yōmu boy fight in Nara and Kashihara; summer scenes around Nara Park appear in the series.
spots.tips: Nara Park's deer are wild animals — feed them only the special deer crackers and watch out for headbutts. The school is modeled on a real high school; don't enter the grounds.

spots.scene: The Taira clashed with the great temples of Nara, ending in Taira no Shigehira burning the city and Tōdai-ji's Great Buddha Hall — a scene the drama portrays.
spots.tips: Tōdai-ji's Great Buddha Hall and the deer of Nara Park are musts; feed deer only special crackers, and mind small children — deer can butt.

spots.scene: The hero returns to "Hitogashima", an island off Wakayama City, for a childhood friend's funeral; the island is modeled on Tomogashima.
spots.tips: Boats leave from Kada port, with few sailings that stop in bad weather. The island has old gun batteries and hilly paths — bring water.

spots.scene: Tokugawa Yoshimune, lord of Kishū, became the eighth shogun and launched the Kyōhō Reforms; his home was Wakayama Castle.
spots.tips: The keep overlooks Wakayama City and the Kinokawa River; the castle's Momijidani garden is a quiet Japanese garden.

spots.scene: Creator Gosho Aoyama was born in Hokuei, Tottori; the museum shows original art and a recreation of his studio, and the town calls itself "Conan Town".
spots.tips: The "Conan Street" from Yura Station to the museum has statues and puzzles along the way. Weekends are busy — go early.

spots.scene: A coming-of-age story of a swim club; the seaside town of Iwatobi is modeled on Iwami in Tottori, whose coast and station appear in the series.
spots.tips: Iwami's Uradome coast is beautiful — take a sightseeing boat past the rock formations. Swim only at official beaches.

spots.scene: After Emperor Go-Daigo escaped from Oki, Nawa Nagatoshi of Hōki sheltered him on Mount Senjō and repelled the shogunate — the episode "The Emperor's Escape" portrays it.
spots.tips: Mount Senjō is known for its screen-like cliffs; the trail is fairly demanding. Cherry blossoms and fresh green at the foot are lovely in spring.

spots.scene: A girl runs all the way to Izumo to meet the eight million gods; Izumo Taisha, Lake Shinji and Matsue all appear in the film.
spots.tips: Izumo Taisha's etiquette is "two bows, four claps, one bow". During Kamiari-zuki (the tenth lunar month) welcoming rites draw big crowds.

spots.scene: The home castle of the Amago, Motonari's greatest rivals; the struggle for Gassan-Toda is the key to his conquest of western Honshu in the drama.
spots.tips: The trails up the mountain castle are steep — wear proper shoes. The top overlooks the Yasugi plain and Lake Naka; the Adachi Museum gardens are nearby.

spots.scene: Prodigy pitcher Harada Takumi and catcher Nagakura Gō, a boys' baseball story set around the Mimasaka region of Okayama.
spots.tips: The tall stone walls of Tsuyama Castle (Kakuzan Park) and its spring blossoms are famous; Tsuyama's hormone udon is the local dish.

spots.scene: Kanbei's plan to flood Bitchū-Takamatsu Castle; in the middle of the siege comes word of the Honnō-ji Incident, launching the drama's great march back east.
spots.tips: The castle site is now a park where you can see the lie of the land used for the dam; a nearby museum explains the flooding siege.

spots.work: In This Corner of the World
spots.scene: Suzu marries into a family in the naval port of Kure and lives an ordinary life through the war; Kure's streets, harbor and warships are drawn in loving detail.
spots.tips: The Yamato Museum tells the story of Kure as a naval port. The slopes and neighborhoods in the film are residential — walk quietly.

spots.scene: Hayao Miyazaki stayed in Tomonoura while developing the film, and the harbor town inspired its seaside setting.
spots.tips: Tomonoura's old port and stone lantern are full of atmosphere; the streets are narrow, so make way for cars and residents. The town is known for Homeishu liqueur.

spots.scene: Taira no Kiyomori was devoted to Itsukushima Shrine and rebuilt it on a grand scale; the great torii in the sea and the corridors symbolize the glory of the Taira.
spots.tips: At low tide you can walk up to the great torii — check the tide tables. Please don't feed the island's deer.

spots.scene: Director Hideaki Anno's hometown is Ube; the station in the film's final scene is Ube-Shinkawa.
spots.tips: There are displays related to the film near the station. It is a working station — don't get in the way of passengers or trains.

spots.scene: In Hōfu in the 1950s, the girl Shinko imagines the Suō provincial capital of a thousand years ago; the wheat fields around the provincial office site are central to the film.
spots.tips: The provincial office site is a historic park next to Hōfu Tenmangū. The wheat fields are farmland — view them from the road.

spots.scene: The heroine is Fumi, sister of Yoshida Shōin, who taught Takasugi Shinsaku, Kusaka Genzui and other Restoration activists at Shōka Sonjuku in Hagi.
spots.tips: Shōka Sonjuku stands in the grounds of Shōin Shrine and is a World Heritage site; Hagi's castle town is great to explore by bicycle.

spots.scene: In this tale of a tanuki family, Shikoku's tanuki legends appear too; Kinchō Shrine in Komatsushima enshrines Kinchō, the legendary tanuki general.
spots.tips: Komatsushima has a giant tanuki statue that makes a great photo spot; please worship quietly at the shrine.

spots.scene: The Miyoshi, who dominate the capital region in the drama, were based at Shōzui Castle in Awa — the clan rose from Awa to march on Kyoto.
spots.tips: The castle site lies around Kenshō-ji temple, with an excavated historic park next to it; Tokushima is also famous for indigo dyeing workshops.

spots.scene: Takagi teases Nishikata every day on Shōdoshima, the author's home island; its shores and ports appear throughout.
spots.tips: Reach Shōdoshima by ferry. The island has a pilgrimage map of the series; drive or cycle safely around it.

spots.scene: The girls of the Hero Club live in Kan'onji, Kagawa, whose seaside and shrines appear again and again.
spots.tips: The Zenigata sand coin carving is best seen from Mount Kotohiki. The school is modeled on a real junior high — don't enter the grounds.

spots.scene: Minamoto no Yoshitsune launched a surprise attack on the Taira at Yashima, scene of the famous moment when Nasu no Yoichi shoots down the fan.
spots.tips: The summit overlooks the old battlefield and the Seto Inland Sea, especially lovely at sunset; Yashima-ji on top is a Shikoku pilgrimage temple.

spots.work: I Want to Eat You, Inhuman (Watashi o Tabetai, Hitodenashi)
spots.scene: A girl living alone meets a 'non-human' girl who says she came from the sea; the seaside town draws partly on the author's home area around Iyo City in Ehime.
spots.tips: Iyo's Futami coast is famous for sunsets, and Shimonada is a well-known seaside station. The station is tiny — don't get in passengers' way on the platform.

spots.scene: The hero, Murata Zōroku (later Ōmura Masujirō), is invited to Uwajima, where he studies Dutch learning and builds an experimental steamship.
spots.tips: Uwajima Castle's keep is one of Japan's original surviving keeps; the stone steps up are steep. Uwajima's sea-bream rice is the local specialty.

spots.scene: A Studio Ghibli coming-of-age film: Taku, now at university in Tokyo, looks back on his high-school days in Kōchi, with the castle and city woven through.
spots.tips: Kōchi Castle's keep and main palace are originals; the Sunday market below the castle is famous.

spots.scene: Sakamoto Ryōma came from Tosa, and the drama begins with his youth there; the Ryōma statue facing the Pacific at Katsurahama and the Ryōma museum are must-sees for fans.
spots.tips: The waves and currents at Katsurahama are strong — swimming is forbidden. The Sakamoto Ryōma Memorial Museum is close by.

spots.scene: Quiet art-club member Sora Kajiwara and her friends sketch their everyday world around Dazaifu in Fukuoka.
spots.tips: Umegae-mochi cakes on the Dazaifu Tenmangū approach are the local treat. Weekends and exam season are crowded — go early.

spots.scene: Late in life Murasaki Shikibu ("Mahiro") travels to Dazaifu, where her husband Nobutaka once served; the drama's closing Kyushu chapter unfolds here.
spots.tips: The site is an open historic park whose foundation stones hint at the old scale; Dazaifu Tenmangū is within walking distance.

spots.scene: Girls revived as zombies form the idol group Franchouchou to revitalize Saga; Karatsu and places across the prefecture appear, and Saga works with the series.
spots.tips: Karatsu Castle overlooks the Niji-no-Matsubara pine grove and Karatsu Bay. Tie-in events are held around the prefecture — follow venue rules.

spots.scene: A Restoration history of Saigō Takamori and Ōkubo Toshimichi that also depicts the Saga Rebellion, raised by Etō Shinpei in the early Meiji years.
spots.tips: The rebuilt palace is a free history museum with guides; the camphor trees along the castle moat are magnificent.

spots.scene: A calligrapher "exiled" to the Gotō Islands finds his own style again amid the island children's mischief; the author is from Gotō.
spots.tips: Reach Gotō by boat or plane. There are many churches on the islands — follow church rules and keep quiet when visiting.

spots.scene: Hitomi, a young witch sent back from 2078 to 2018, rediscovers color among Nagasaki's slopes, harbor and Western-style houses.
spots.tips: Nagasaki is all slopes — wear comfortable shoes. The houses around Glover Garden overlook the harbor; the night view is famous too.

spots.scene: In Nagasaki Ryōma founded Kameyama Shachū, Japan's first trading company; it is the base for the drama's later Nagasaki chapters.
spots.tips: The museum sits in a hillside residential area up the stone steps of "Ryōma Street" — please be quiet among the homes.

spots.scene: Natsume, who can see yōkai, and his cat Nyanko-sensei; the author is from Kumamoto, and the countryside around Hitoyoshi and Kuma is one of its models.
spots.tips: Hitoyoshi has a pilgrimage map of the series; the Kuma River and Aoi Aso Shrine are well worth seeing.

spots.work: Diary of Our Days at the Breakwater
spots.scene: A girl who moves to a seaside town joins the "breakwater club" and learns to fish; the town is modeled on the Ashikita area of Kumamoto.
spots.tips: Wear a life jacket when fishing from the breakwater, watch for big waves, stay out of closed piers, and take your rubbish and bait home.

spots.scene: Kanakuri Shisō, Japan's first Olympic marathon runner and hero of the drama's first half, was born in Nagomi, Kumamoto; his birthplace is one of its settings.
spots.tips: The museum tells his life story; at certain times of year the nearby Futamata bridges cast a heart-shaped shadow at noon.

spots.scene: Negishi Sōichi dreams of trendy pop but ends up fronting a death-metal band; his family home is in Inukai, Ōita.
spots.tips: Inukai is a quiet town on the Ōno River; Harajiri Falls and Chinda Falls are nearby.

spots.scene: After the conquest of Kyushu Kanbei received Buzen and built Nakatsu Castle — the drama's "Nakatsu in Buzen" chapter.
spots.tips: The castle stands at the mouth of the Yamakuni River; its walls show both Kuroda- and Hosokawa-era masonry. Nakatsu fried chicken is famous.

spots.scene: In the first episode the story begins at a rural hospital in Miyazaki, and shrines and scenery around Takachiho appear.
spots.tips: Boats in Takachiho Gorge have long queues — plan ahead in peak season. Yokagura night dances are a local tradition; watch quietly.

spots.scene: At the end of the Satsuma Rebellion, Saigō disbanded his army near Kitagawa in Nobeoka, burned his uniform and broke out over Mount Enodake.
spots.tips: Mount Enodake has hiking trails but they are rough — go in company and carry water. Nobeoka also has a museum at Saigō's last camp.

spots.scene: The robotics club of Tanegashima Central High dreams of building a giant robot; the island's space center and coast are the story's stage.
spots.tips: The space center's science museum is free; on launch days the island is packed, so book lodging early.

spots.scene: At the end of the Satsuma Rebellion, Saigō Takamori fell back to Shiroyama in his home town of Kagoshima, where his life ended.
spots.tips: The Shiroyama lookout faces Sakurajima across Kinkō Bay; the hill has the Saigō cave and other sites — watch for snakes and bees on the paths.

spots.scene: Two girls meet at a small aquarium in Okinawa, in Nanjō in the south of the main island.
spots.tips: Nanjō has the World Heritage site Sēfa-utaki, a sacred place of prayer — keep silent and don't touch the rocks or offerings.

spots.scene: Set when Satsuma invaded the Ryukyu Kingdom in the 17th century; Shuri Castle, the royal palace, is the drama's center stage.
spots.tips: The main hall is being rebuilt after the 2019 fire, and the restoration work can be viewed. There are many slopes — guard against heat in summer.
